maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF PRESIDENT OF AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of recent press reports I would like to make a brief statement.
A few weeks ago Mr. Charles Gavsie, president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, advised me that for almost a year he had been considering accepting a position with a private law firm in Montreal and that the time was rapidly approaching when he must make a decision in this matter. He advised me he would like to resign his position as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority on January 31 next and enter the law firm on that date.
In spite of my best efforts to persuade him to at least postpone this decision until after the opening of the seaway, he thought he could not do so without jeopardizing the opportunity now afforded him, and for this reason he is tendering his resignation effective January 31, 1958.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke asked the following question:
Has the government become aware of heavy imports of hay from the United States of America into western and southern British Columbia, mainly delivered by trucks and trailers? If so, is any action contemplated to protect the hay growers of the Okanagan and Shuswap areas, who find it impossible to meet this competition?
The answer is as follows. The government is aware of the fact that hay is being imported into southern British Columbia. This is a normal situation because certain parts of that province, such as the Fraser valley and the Cariboo, usually are deficit areas for hay. The volume of imports varies widely from year to year, depending on local crop and pasture conditions.
From January to August, 1956, imports amounted to 27,805 tons. During the same months of 1957 imports amounted to 19,702 tons. While complete official import figures are not available for subsequent months this year, present indications are that imports will be substantially lower than they were in the same months last year.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Recent reports from British Columbia indicate that a substantial part of current imports is being carried by truck, but again no complete current statistics are available.
Market reports indicate that imported alfalfa hay of good quality is being delivered to Williams Lake at about $31 per ton and to Vancouver at from $26.75 to $27 per ton. Rail freight from the northern Okanagan and Shuswap is approximately $11.40 per ton; hence alfalfa hay of good quality originating in the north Okanagan area and shipped to Vancouver should be worth between $15 and $16 per ton at the shipping point.
An estimate made by the provincial department of agriculture indicates a surplus of about 1,500 tons of hay in the north Okanagan and Shuswap areas, but it is also indicated that these areas normally ship very little hay to the coastal region. In any event the amount available seems to be very much less than will be required, particularly for the dairy herds in the lower mainland.
In view of these facts and estimates and of the admitted urgent need of both dairy farmers and beef cattle producers for additional supplies of hay, it would not appear desirable to consider any restrictions or controls on imports of hay at the present time. In addition, of course, there is at present no legal basis for such action. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary sent in a similar question.

Wholesale quotations at Vancouver during the above period in 1957 per 100 pounds of

Inquiries of the Ministry No. 1 grade ranged from $2.90-$3.35 for domestic potatoes and from $3.25-$3.50 for United States potatoes. Comparable prices a year ago were $3.15-$3.65 for domestic and $2.85-$4.65 for imported potatoes.
Imports of United States potatoes must meet the requirements of Canada No. 1 grade, or the equivalent of United States No. 1 grade. In addition, all such imports during this period were dutiable at 37J cents per 100 pounds.

Mr. Speaker, on November 19 the hon. member for Cartier addressed the following question to me:
Can the minister tell the house whether any member states of the United Nations have violated or are violating the request of the United Nations not to send military equipment to the Middle East?
I took that question as notice, Mr. Speaker, and I regret my tardiness in replying to the question but I was at the United Nations last week.
Before addressing myself to the substantive part of the question of the hon. member for Cartier I might first correct the misapprehension implicit in the wording of this question regarding the area to which the United Nations resolution was intended to apply. That resolution was not applicable to the whole area of the Middle East, but only to that part of it in which hostilities were taking place at that time, namely Israel and Egypt.
Turning now to the question of whether other United Nations member states are observing the United Nations recommendation, I can only say that it would obviously be a tremendous task for the Canadian government to attempt to keep track of the attitudes and activities of the other 81 fellow United Nations members. It is no secret that there have been deliveries of significant military equipment to the area in question by members of the Soviet bloc, and there have been press reports about deliveries from other countries. However, as I pointed out in my statement of November 19, the Canadian decision to observe the spirit of the United Nations recommendation is not determined by the example of others but rests upon a combination of respect for a United Nations resolution and national considerations relating to our participation in the United Nations emergency force.

On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I want to address a question to the Postmaster General, now colonel in chief of philately and a former caustic opposition critic of the postal engraver's art. With respect to the stamp to be issued as a tribute to the contribution of the press to the development of Canada, does the minister consider it appropriate that Canada should be stood on end to achieve this objective?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. It immediately occurred to me that this stamp is just one other example of the many things stood on end by the previous government which my colleagues and I have been straightening out to their proper relationship.
I made inquiries, Mr. Speaker, and I am informed that this stamp, the design of which was approved in April preceding the election; and the colour, which is that black so regretted by many people using stamps, which was approved in May preceding the election, hardly come within the purview of this government. I also understand, Mr. Speaker, that the design, including the stood on end Canada, had the approval of certain advisers of the department who are considered qualified in matters of art.
In reference to this particular stamp, Mr. Speaker, and in reference to some of the comments we have heard in the past, I may say that we are considering somewhat of a broadening of the group of advisers to be consulted about designs in the future.

May I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In the five months since June 21 has the Postmaster General not had time to stop this issue if he felt the way in which he has described it in the house?

I was
hoping someone would ask that question, Mr. Speaker; that is why I left one point unanswered. The stamp was originally intended for issue in October; therefore it went into production immediately following approval of the plate and the colour before this government moved into office and we had a chance to review these things. The reason it was not issued in October, and it now stands ready for issue-printed, of course-has been that the stamp commemorating the royal visit was used to replace this stamp, and it is now intended to release this stamp in January.

I should like to direct a question to the Postmaster General. I did not send him notice of the question, but I judge he will know the answer. Will the stamps in the future have larger numerals on them than in the past? Also will the stamps of certain denominations all be of the one colour?

As
to the size of the numerals on stamps, something which has been a matter of concern to the hon. member for Peterborough for some time, may I say that these numerals are being enlarged. I might also say in this connection that we are currently in consultation, and have been over the last month or so, with an expert on the question of lettering generally so the lettering included on our stamps might be as satisfactory as possible.
Generally, where possible, we will try to follow a standard colour pattern for stamps, but very often that proves to be difficult. A case in point is the special issue which received so much commendation, commemorating the royal visit. The selection of the colour was dictated by the fact that this design was based on a photograph and was intended to represent a photographic technique, and therefore black and white was the appropriate colour for that particular stamp. But generally an attempt will be made to follow a standard colour pattern.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I desire to congratulate you upon your election as presiding officer of this house. With your host of friends across Canada I felicitate the house on your elevation. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I desire to address some remarks to the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson). I congratulate him on the unique distinction that has come to him in the award of the Nobel peace prize. He has brought recognition to himself and great prestige to Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that the award to him has made my task no easier, but having that in mind I still congratulate him and share the joy of Canadians in that award.
It is indeed a great privilege for me to represent Hastings-Frontenac in this house, an area which is so distinguished in the founding and building of Canada, and I say to my constituents that I will endeavour to be worthy of the support they accorded me. I am not unaware of the fact that the parties in this house did not contest the by-election, and I have only this to observe, that I trust it is the beginning of a habit with respect to this.
I know the people of this country are indeed interested in the foreign policy of Canada, our actions and policies in the field of external affairs, and I also know that other governments are equally interested in the actions and policies of this government. We have been considering in this house, and we shall be considering in this house, matters of great moment which might be described as domestic or national. I am not discounting in any measure the importance and significance of these matters when I observe that the solution of the grave problems which

External Affairs
confront the nations of the world in 1957 has a practical bearing on the health and happiness of Canadians and on the welfare and progress of Canada.
We cannot expect in this field of external affairs to find ready made solutions. Only the eradication of fear and the establishment of mutual confidence among the nations will provide the basic solution, and the government will endeavour in every way to bring this about. Second, to bring about this state of affairs we shall need steadiness, strength and patience.
In view of the fact that today I am making my first statement on foreign policy, and having regard to the fact that there are many new members of the house, freshmen like myself, I propose to outline in somewhat general terms some of the relations and relationships of Canada with other nations. In common with Canadians of all political persuasions I take pride in the advancement of our country to a position of respect and influence in the international field. We are regarded as a leading country of middle-status in the world. Our role is an important one in the commonwealth, in the affairs of the United Nations, in NATO and in all the other various organizations to which Canada adheres. That is a position which Canada has attained by reason of its growing strength, its sense of responsibility and its willingness to accept responsibility; and I believe it is also due to the exercise by Canadians of a certain wisdom and maturity of judgment.
Natural resources and the development of those resources which Canada has achieved have helped to give us a prestige out of all proportion to the size of our population. Our sacrifices in two world wars, and then in recent years in securing the peace in Korea, the Middle East and Indo-China, have added to that prestige; our contributions, of which I will speak later, toward raising the standard of living in various parts of the world, and our contributions toward the alleviation of want and suffering have, too, enabled Canada to speak with confidence and authority.
Moreover, I think we bring to the consideration of the solution of international problems peculiar qualities which Canadians possess. We are the heirs of a European civilization, and I would think, having regard to the development of our national scene that we have a national, or perhaps I should say a natural, tendency and gift for compromise. We are possessed of an idealism which has been somewhat modified by the skepticism which Canadians must have when they realize that the solution of any problem cannot come about by miracles but only as the result of persistent and hard endeavour.
[Mr. Smith (Hastings-Frontenac) .1
And so, Mr. Speaker, it is with these encouraging yet challenging thoughts in mind that I take up my new office as Secretary of State for External Affairs. As I enter this field I assure this house that having regard to the firm foundations which have been laid in respect of our foreign affairs by successive governments I will endeavour to build on these foundations and, as a member of this government under the leadership of the Prime Minister, I will do my best to help in building something distinctive and valuable upon these foundations.
In this context it is clear that Canada must seek to understand the aspirations of other countries; Canada must endeavour to apprehend the motives of other nations, whether they be ill or good, and work closely with friendly nations. But all the while Canadians must think for themselves, and Canada's foreign policy should not be merely a pale reflection of the views of other countries.
My first assignment after I became a member of the government was to go to the United Nations. I think that was an excellent introduction for me because it enabled me to study at first hand, at the beginning of my political and diplomatic career, the machinery, the aspirations and the objectives of that great organization.
'j'hgi'g was in the United Nations, I found, a curiosity with respect to the attitude of the new government in Canada toward the organization, and I can best describe the views of this government by repeating to this house the words of the Prime Minister when he spoke to the general assembly on September 3, 1957. He stated: "We stand on this question now where Canada has always stood since April, 1945. And I emphasize this, with the support of the party which is now in power. So far as Canada is concerned, support of the United Nations is a cornerstone of its foreign policy. We believe that the United Nations will grow stronger because it represents the inevitable struggle of countries to find order in their relationships, and the deep longing of mankind to strive for and attain peace and justice." That is the stand of this country toward the United Nations.
Our confidence in the United Nations, Mr. Speaker, is not blind. It is, we know, an imperfect instrument. Yet one can understand that. The United Nations is not, as the secretary general stated in his last annual report, a supra-state, and how can we expect the United Nations to be better than those who constitute it? The United Nations is, indeed, a microcosm of an imperfect world, a world now in the shadow of nuclear weapons. However, the United Nations has had

its successes, and I think it warrants the designation or description that it is the work shop of world diplomacy.
And amidst all the portents and dark threats of 1957, I suggest to you, sir, that the United Nations is the greatest hope for peace. If the United Nations were not in existence I do think mankind would have to invent something like it in order to afford a forum in which 82 nations could sit down together and discuss face to face their differences and their agreements.
It is a gratifying yet a sobering thought for us that Canada will take its seat for the second time on the security council. That will happen on January 1, 1958.
I was particularly pleased that my first task at the United Nations was to endorse the admission of Malaya and to welcome that country as the newest member state of that organization. The United Nations has now become a more universal body, and many of its new members have risen from the status of colony to that of nationhood. It afforded me even greater pleasure to say on that occasion that I saluted Great Britain, because here was another case that we in Canada know so well of Great Britain encouraging a colony to become a nation. I could not refrain from observing that this had been the historic, the outstanding record of Great Britain, while the U.S.S.R. reversed that process of developing colonies into nations by reducing nations to colonies.
Canada has worked and will continue to work with these new members of the United Nations, and as far as my experience is concerned it has been a joy to co-operate with them.
Among the topics which were discussed at the United Nations this year was the question of disarmament, which was perhaps the major topic. I and members of my delegation at the United Nations had some reason to be not entirely satisfied about the consideration in the twelfth session of the United Nations of that topic which means so much to mankind. The 24 powers did put forward a resolution that was drafted by the subcommittee on disarmament on August 29, 1957, and that resolution did receive en-dorsation by the general assembly. In fact the U.S.S.R. was not able to line up any votes in opposition to that resolution except those of its own satellites. It is true that there were some who abstained from voting on that 24-power resolution, but I judged that in many cases the abstention was due not to any opposition to the resolution but because they really thought any resolution put forward and adopted by the United Nations would be ineffective as the U.S.S.R. said they would not co-operate in further negotiations under that resolution.
External Affairs
Would you mind stating the resolution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have it here but it is quite long. Could I offer it as a paper to be put in my speech? It would take about five minutes to read, Mr. Speaker, but I could outline its purport. It is to the effect that we should make a partial step in disarmament.
After we had obtained for that resolution approval from the general assembly which was unanimous but with abstentions, the U.S.S.R. said they would not participate in the discussions of the disarmament commission or of the subcommittee. We were greatly disappointed to hear that, because in getting that resolution so admirably supported in the United Nations we felt we had a vote of the peoples of the world that would carry some weight with the U.S.S.R. because it reflected a world-wide opinion that they should consider the rejection of the western proposals.
We tried to make it clear to the United Nations that the resolution that was so widely supported in the general assembly was not necessarily in our opinion the only means whereby disarmament could be promoted. On October 23, 1957, I spoke in the political committee and asked our soviet friends to look at the resolution; not to regard it as coming from us in a take it or leave it manner, but to accept it on our assurance that it would be a basis for further negotiations. Well, after the U.S.S.R. stated definitely that they would not negotiate any further, they did put forward the suggestion that the disarmament commission should be made up of the 82 member nations of the United Nations, and indeed that the complexion of the general assembly itself should be reflected in the new disarmament commission.
We all felt that this was a manifestly impractical proposition, and we were bound to conclude that it was merely a propaganda move. It would be entirely unwieldy for 82 nations to sit down and discuss the problem in one meeting or series of meetings on disarmament. That was, however, put to the general assembly by the U.S.S.R. and it was rejected by the general assembly.
Even after that Canada, taking the lead in some cases and in other cases co-operating with other friendly powers, tried again to find a well-balanced and reasonable group by way of a suggestion for the composition of the disarmament commission that would satisfy the U.S.S.R. Finally there was put before the general assembly a proposal for

External Affairs
the extension and enlargement of the disarmament commission to include the members of the security council, 11, and Canada, and in addition 14 other countries. That was adopted by the general assembly to the extent that three-quarters of the governments of every group in the United Nations endorsed it. That proved unacceptable to the U.S.S.R., although at one point in our negotiations we did hope that it might be acceptable to them.
Now that the enlarged disarmament commission has been established the U.S.S.R. say they will not participate in its discussions and our only hope is that they will reconsider their views so we can sit down together with them to the end that the armament race will not be continued, because as I endeavoured to tell the political committee of the United Nations-and I have no desire to indulge in scare headlines here today-the issue is in effect and in essence human survival.
In all these arguments in the committee and in the general assembly the Russians came back time and time again to their proposal. The first part of their counterproposal is that the nations of the world who are members of the U.N. should resolve to ban the use of nuclear weapons. Since I have come to Ottawa I have had letters from many persons throughout Canada which said, "What a laudable proposal that is from the U.S.S.R."
Now, sir, one must confess it has an immediate attraction and appeal. "Ban the use of nuclear weapons." I ask you, sir, and I ask this house why, then, can we not accept this laudable proposal? The answer, the grim answer, is that a promise not to use nuclear weapons is good only until one nation decides to break it. There must be, for our security, a measure of inspection that will ensure that the undertakings in that regard are being carried out. Disarmament cannot be achieved by the stroke of a pen or the mere passing of a resolution.
My colleague the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) who was vice-chairman of the Canadian delegation at the twelfth session of the assembly, took a very active part in these negotiations, and I know he will be ready and willing to amplify what I have endeavoured to tell the house this afternoon.
In addition to disarmament, a striking characteristic of the debate had to do with the words I used a few moments ago, "human survival". It is evident that the advances or discoveries in the field of science and technology pose a new and urgent problem in international politics. We cannot solve that problem merely by talking about our endeavours of yesteryear. New scientific

weapons and scientific discoveries have provided an urgency about the solution of those problems. Canada, I can assure this house, will endeavour in every way possible to advance further discussion and negotiations with respect to disarmament. For 11 years representatives of Canada have carried on those endeavours, and we hope we can keep the Canadian flag waving in respect of a matter of such vital concern to the human race, at least to make suggestions in negotiating a first-stage agreement with the U.S.S.R.
Apart from disarmament there was consideration of political crises. One had to do particularly with Syria. The Syrians lodged a resolution with the secretary general that would provide for a discussion of the threat to their security on the Syrian-Turkish border. Several efforts were made toward negotiation in that regard. I was there when the debate opened and I can still remember the polemics and the propaganda that were indulged in by the chief delegate for the U.S.S.R. Our approach to that problem was that any nation such as Syria should have the opportunity to bring before the general assembly what it thought was a threat to its security. That did not in any way indicate that we had in mind that Turkey as a responsible member of NATO would act in an irresponsible way. But we endeavoured to provide every possible way of finding out the facts.
Hon. members may recall that King Saud of Saudi Arabia offered to intervene and mediate, and there were suggestions that the security council might come into the picture. In association with Japan, Denmark, Norway, Paraguay, Peru and Spain we put forward a resolution that would call attention to the availability of the secretary general for consultation between Syria and Turkey, or even the availability of the secretary general to carry on an investigation; and then rather dramatically Syria and Turkey decided that the debate should be terminated.
I said it was dramatic, but it was not very spectacular. I do not think the press gave it enough publicity. It really was a product of what the secretary general of the United Nations has said of the United Nations "diplomacy of reconciliation." There in the general assembly these charges and countercharges were exchanged, and it was undoubtedly felt by the U.S.S.R. that it was up to Syria in this regard; that they were losing the battle of polemics and that their propaganda concepts and objectives were being turned against them. That was indeed a victory for the United Nations and for the participation of the nations of the world in that debate in the general assembly.

* It would be an illusion, Mr. Speaker, to think that the underlying causes of tension in that area, and the fever and the rise in tempers, are gone. We would all hope that the diplomacy, the reconciliation which was provided by the United Nations could be again brought to bear on the lowering of the fever and on the lowering of tempers.
I now desire to say something about the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East. Notwithstanding press reports today with respect to another sector, the Jordanian-Israeli border, of which we in the department as yet have nothing more than we have read in the paper, I can say that the record of UNEF, the United Nations emergency force, has been one of great satisfaction not only to the U.N. but to the world. There have been on the border few incidents in recent months. Indeed, I was talking to Major General Burns and he told me that in the last few weeks there have not been any incidents on that border. Undoubtedly UNEF contributed at least to arrest the movement that might have resulted in war, and we in Canada must be proud of our participation in that force. One-fifth of the force come from Canada, 1,200 out of 6,000. We must take a particular pride in the commander in chief of the force, Major General E. L. M. Burns. On all sides he was praised by members of the general assembly in the debate that took place last Friday morning. I would say, in the words of our Prime Minister who spoke to the general assembly in September, that as long as the United Nations considers the presence of the UNEF in that particular area as necessary, Canada will continue to support by participating in its composition.
The secretary general in his recent annual report, having mentioned the temporary nature of the force, with the limited mandate in a particular area, went on to say that the value of such a force in such situations has been fully demonstrated. I would certainly subscribe to that view, as all the delegations from the west would. In that report the secretary general suggested that an agreed stand-by plan for a United Nations peace force which could be activated on short notice might be given consideration. Small wars, small conflicts, expand into great wars, and if agreement could be reached on the establishment of such a force I would think it would be a most significant step in making the United Nations a more effective organization for the maintenance of peace.
The establishment of the United Nations emergency force as an experiment gave rise to certain consequences, and one had to do with money. The estimated cost of the force during the period from November, 1956, to 96698-97
External Affairs
December 31, 1957 is in the region of $30 million. Against this sum the total amount received or firmly pledged so far is some $24 million. That includes the recent offer from the United States of $12 million and the recent offer from the United Kingdom of $1 million. It now appears that there will be a shortfall for the period ending December 31, 1957, of approximately $3 million to $4 million. It is estimated that in the year 1958 the force will cost $25 million.
I have used these figures, and I do not regard them as large or high when you put into the balance the great benefit that has followed the establishment and deployment of that force on that border, the release of tension thereby preventing further expansion of the conflict in the area. On Friday last I introduced in the general assembly a resolution for which 20 other countries offered their co-sponsorship. That resolution reaffirmed the principle that the responsibility for additional funds required in 1958 for the maintenance of this force should be shared by all members of the United Nations in accordance with the scale of assessment that is invoked for the normal United Nations budget. That resolution was adopted despite the opposition of the U.S.S.R. bloc, and was adopted by a larger majority than we expected, with the result that I can say to members of the house that the financing of UNEF is now assured.
Other Middle East isues continue to be the centre of attention at the United Nations. One of them has to do with the grave plight of the Palestinian refugees, and in this context one cannot say that any real progress has been made during the past year. The United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees in the Near East, to give it its full title, has continued to provide essential rations and other relief services, but shortage of funds has increasingly hampered the agency in its effort to maintain these services or to proceed in an orderly way with the limited rehabilitation projects possible under present conditions.
I am happy to report that Canada during the past nine years has been the fourth largest non-Arab contributor to Palestine refugee relief, and in 1957 Canada was the third largest contributor. We have continued to urge other countries that they should accord greater support to UNRWA in order that there will not be a further decline in the standard of living of these unfortunate refugees. The estimates for 1957-58, at present before the house, seek approval of a Canadian contribution to UNRWA of $750,000 to cover the 18-month period ending December 31, 1957. When the estimates for

External Affairs
1958-59 are brought before the next session, parliament will be asked to approve a Canadian contribution to UNRWA, of $500,000, which is relatively the same as the figure of $750,000 in relation to 18 months.
Before I turn from the United Nations I desire to inform the house of certain other contributions to the United Nations extrabudgetary programs. The following amounts are included in the 1957-58 estimates at present before the house to cover Canadian contributions to these programs of the United Nations during the calendar year 1957. In the 1958-59 estimates parliament will be asked by the government to approve Canadian contributions of the same amounts to cover the programs of these organizations during the year 1958.
These are the amounts. In addition to UNRWA there is $2 million to the United Nations expanded program of technical assistance, $200,000 to the United Nations refugee fund and $650,000 to the United Nations children's emergency fund. All these proposed contributions are on the same scale as those to which the previous parliament gave its approval.
I turn now, for want of time but not for want of subject matter, from the United Nations to another vitally important sector of our foreign policy.

Would the minister permit a question? I wonder whether the minister could assure the house that notwithstanding Canada's negative vote in the economic and social council, Canada will support the SUNFED program which is currently being debated in the general assembly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

I am very happy to respond to that question. There are negotiations going on now at the United Nations-the Minister of Finance referred to this in the house last week-with respect to the providing of financial assistance outside of the Colombo plan to nations not only in southeast and south Asia but throughout the world. I would ask the hon. member to believe me when I say that I do not regard the negative vote against the proposal of SUNFED as indicating that the Canadian government will not support a proposal that I hope will come out of the negotiations.
Those negotiations are still being carried on and, as the Minister of Finance stated, the government has not yet heard of their results and has, of course, made no decision. When the decision in that regard is made the government will quickly inform the house. Without going into the details-and it would not be fitting for me to disclose the details of

negotiations-I think perhaps another proposal will be even more helpful to these underdeveloped countries than the particular SUNFED plan.
If I may leave the United Nations and go to the Colombo plan, I doubt, Mr. Speaker, whether there is any single task in the international field which Canada has undertaken that should receive greater approval and endorsation from Canadians of all walks of life and all political persuasions. No reasonable man could doubt the benefits which this type of enterprise is bringing to all of us in the western world, in the non-communist world, to put it that way, whether we are benefactors or whether we are beneficiaries of the operation of the Colombo plan.
Two of my colleagues in the government have recently been in south and southeast Asia, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne). They have returned to Ottawa, and from each of them I have heard of the unceasing struggle of the undeveloped countries in that part of the world to raise their standards of living. The hon. member for St. John's West, who attended in my place the Saigon meeting of the consultative committee of the Colombo plan, can testify to the benefits that have accrued from Canada's investment in these particular projects.
These grants, hon. members of the house -and I say this from the bottom of my being-are not hand-outs. We should really think of them as helping hands. There is another feature, members of the house, about our investment in the Colombo plan. Famine, distress and low standards of living create the seed-beds of unrest and indeed could create-and in some instances have done so-the seed-bed of war. It worries me to talk in this vein, but if anyone wants to talk about these matters in mere monetary terms, I would offer a good argument and, I think, a conclusive one that in time these countries in which we are making investments will become good customers and provide much opportunity for Canada. But I put that suggestion forward in second or third place.
As some hon. members of this house know, particularly the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), the Colombo plan was a concept initiated and brought about in the commonwealth. Here is another instance of the commonwealth creating a nucleus which in due course produced a strengthened, forward-looking and beneficial international enterprise. In the routine aspect of carrying forward the program under the Colombo plan there always has had to be and there will

have to be discussions with engineers, administrators and economists. Then there will have to be discussions with the countries to whom help might be offered, as to their needs. When decisions in that regard are made, Mr. Speaker, we will of course report to the house.
On November 22 in this session of parliament the Prime Minister informed the house that the government will seek parliamentary approval of an appropriation for 1958-59 of $35 million. The estimates that will be considered in a few days provide for a contribution of $34,400,000. We are proposing an increase of $600,000 for 1958-59.
Time does not permit me to go into detail with respect to other parts of south and southeast Asia but in passing I would refer to the work of the international commissions in Indochina. The task of the commission in Cambodia is, in our opinion, about completed. There have been difficulties in the way of dissolving or disbanding the commission. In Laos where we are members of an international commission, after nearly three years of negotiations between the royal government and the Pathet Lao, an agreement has finally been reached whereby the Pathet Lao which has been controlling one part of Laos will be integrated into the national community. I seize this opportunity to say that we sympathize with the desire of the Laotian people to achieve a political settlement within the terms of the Geneva agreements of 1954. We hope that this latest development will result in a strong Laos and a continuation of the democratic approach that has been followed by the royal government.
Viet-Nam remains divided. It is in this area where the sort of international supervision that is provided by the international commissions has been most important for the maintenance of peace.
In relation to south and southeast Asia I would reiterate what I have endeavoured to say, namely that the recent visits of ministers of the government to that part of the world should be taken as indicative of our interest in the area, our close interest in commonwealth ties, our desire to help the countries of the area to improve their standard of living and of our willingness to do our part in preserving peace.
A few moments ago I mentioned the commonwealth. May I interpolate here-and this is a personal note-that after I reached the United Nations in the middle of September I was asked to attend a meeting of the commonwealth group. It was not a bloc but a group. I am sure that no one else in the room could appreciate how thrilled I was, 96698-97i
External Affairs
indeed how excited I was, at that first meeting. Here sitting around a horseshoe table were representatives of ten independent nations of the British commonwealth, men and women coming from various climes, of various religions and cultures. There they sat. It seemed to me-and this is the basis of my thrill and of my excitement-that there was before me a brilliant page of British history, the bringing of colonies to nationhood. There was no treaty binding them together. Indeed I would say, for the want of a better word, that there was something mystical in their adherence to common ideals of the dignity of the individual, of justice, fairness and fair play.
I now come closer to home, Mr. Speaker, and I desire for a moment or two to mention our neighbours in this hemisphere. I would point out first our relationship to the republics of Latin America. Some of my first conversations at the United Nations in September were with representatives of the republics of Latin America. Since I have been in Ottawa I am gradually beginning to get to know better the ambassadors from Latin America. I know that in the assembly and the councils of the United Nations our Canadian representatives over the years have acquired a deep appreciation of the strength, the wisdom and the vision which representatives of the Latin republics have brought to the discussions, deliberations and decisions of that body.
I refer, just by way of example, to only two. Colombia and Brazil made contributions in men and equipment to UNEF. Colombia and Brazil have each served three times on the security council. I think of Brazil today, which is the largest Latin nation in the world, with a population larger than that of Spain or Italy or France, with enormous natural resources scarcely tapped, a country of great promise. We have traded with those countries over many years, indeed for a century I am informed. I hope that the substantial volume of our two-way trade with the Latin American nations today is only a stage on the way to greater expansion.
But it is only in the post-war years since 1945 that there has been an increased exchange of personnel, visitors and businessmen between Canada and the Latin American republics. Attending our colleges and universities are a considerable number of students who have come to us from Latin America. Visitors and tourists are increasing. Commercial aviation has been a significant factor in helping us to become better acquainted with the Latin American countries. The Mexican air line operates a regular service

External Affairs
between Mexico City and Windsor, Ontario. Our own Canadian Pacific Air Lines now ranks as a major air service in the Americas. Those 20 independent nations are playing an increasing part in deliberations that are designed for the solution of international problems-and I express the hope that the cordial relations which now exist with those 20 nations will be enhanced and increased.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to our closest neighbour, the United States. A kindly providence has willed the geographical location of that country with respect to Canada. With the United States we share a continent and a common heritage from many lands beyond the seas, moulded around political philosophies which have become, in some measure perhaps, the central core of the institutions of both our countries. These philosophies, coming from our twin motherlands, Great Britain and France, have been shared by us as comrades in arms during two world wars. Again, when we fought with the Americans under the flag of the United Nations in Korea, we Canadians knew the value of our American friends.
We have been in close association with our neighbour in the United Nations and we also work closely with them in NATO. Particularly those of us who remember the years before the first world war, welcome their assumption of world leadership during the last two decades. I must however observe that sometimes in pursuit of common objectives the means chosen by the United States to effect these ends may have side effects which are injurious to Canada and which in many instances are not made clear to the American people and of which therefore they are not properly aware.
When we in Canada consider that such effects may stem from any action or inaction on the part of the United States and may affect what we deem to be the best and just interests of our country and our people we must, without petulance or sophomoric sensitivity, seek from our United States neighbours the consideration of those effects. There is nothing wrong or improper with conscientiously facing the problems or difficulties separating true friends. This is also true in the field of international relations. What to my mind would be wrong and improper would be for us to dig and dig for slights and to magnify oversights. It would be equally wrong on the part of Canada and equally improper for the two governments to allow old and burning problems to fester, if I may use that word, and to continue unresolved. It is in that way that misunderstandings grow and fair-mindedness of the people and their governments may be warped. There have been problems between our 
countries throughout our history. The territorial part which we know as Canada did not exist in the early days but those who have read the biography of Sir John A. Macdonald by Professor Creighton will appreciate what I have been saying.
From those early years there have been problems between us and they have continued, indeed, down to our present difficulties with respect to the United States wheat surplus disposal programs. I declare, Mr. Speaker, that considerate frankness will not endanger true friendship between our countries. Above all, it is of paramount importance to international peace that Canada and the United States, unequal as they are with respect to military and economic force but equal in their common respect for the dignity of the individual, should set a continued example to the whole world of how friendly nations can live together.
May I state as simply as I can how I see the development of our relations with the United States. We must be friends; friendship however means something more than the absence of enmity. Friendship really means the existence of positive and effective interest on the part of each nation in the welfare of the other.
In recent weeks we have been dramatically stopped in our tracks; we have been forced to give closer examination to our collective security arrangements by reason of the success of the U.S.S.R. in the launching of the intercontinental ballistic missile and in the launching of two earth satellites. It has been a shock but it has had a salutary effect in terms of the re-appraisal of our common defence.
We in the democracies are apt to relax until pressure is brought upon us by the course of events; then we jump into action. I do think that in this age of infinite risk we should have some concern about this characteristic tendency to relax in the absence of pressure. That attitude of relaxation when there is no pressure on us may, and in this case probably has, tempted fate. However, we have now been dramatically reminded of the terrible menace of nuclear warfare and as a result all members of NATO recognize they are faced with the necessity of making far-reaching decisions in the military field while, at the same time, having to cope with political problems of exceptional complexity. I claim your indulgence at this time as I desire to make a careful statement in this regard. I wish to say a word about military and political problems because I think the success of NATO in rising to the occasion will depend largely on how it can merge its military and its political objectives.

Despite soviet accusations that NATO is an aggressor and was designed for aggression, the sole military purpose of NATO-this has been declaimed over and over again and we have no reason to doubt it-is to deter aggression by providing firm evidence that aggressors would be quickly and successfully met if they should attack any member of the alliance. In NATO there is a formidable capability-as General Norstad stated in Ottawa 10 days ago-to deter aggression. In this connection he also said that this capability is not altered or modified by the possession by any other power of a nuclear intercontinental ballistic missile.
This is a field, I am aware, where theories abound and often conflict. I do not intend to do more at this point than to state the government's position, indeed its conviction, that the value of NATO as a deterrent remains intact and that it is incumbent upon us-we who have banded together in NATO -to exploit the opportunities which exist for closer co-operation in the fields of military, economic and scientific affairs.
We must seek for co-operation by increased exchange of scientific and technical information and from the stimulation of scientific education and research in the NATO countries. We should be able to find that further co-operation is possible in the economic production of modern weapons.
Military problems will loom large on the agenda of the NATO meeting which is to be held next month in Paris but, in the minds of many governments and of many peoples, that meeting will be judged just as much by its achievement in the non-military field as in the military field and, with the challenge of communism all the time advancing, NATO must move with the times in the field of politics.
It is dreadfully essential that we of the NATO alliance should intensify and develop our military contribution. But that is not enough. It is essential that we should work together to improve our machinery for consultation and promote the intimacy of our intramural understanding. These obligations are with us and they must be observed, but they are limited. To confine ourselves in NATO to attaining them alone would be to cultivate our own interdependence as members of NATO without realizing that the health and strength of the alliance depends on its relations with the world outside. There is, in other words, a global interdependence in this age of scientific discovery and nationalist ferment, and it is important for us and important for NATO not to underestimate that need.
No one should think of letting down his guard at the present time; no prudent man
External Affairs
can deny the need for defence insurance. What I am suggesting is that the security organization will be successful or unsuccessful according to the degree of intelligence with which its political policies are formulated and pursued.
To give an example, I turn for a moment to the problem of soviet activity in uncommitted neutral states. This is a serious and growing danger. How are they going? Are they going toward the soviets or toward the west? This cannot be ignored by NATO members, and yet NATO as such is perhaps not well equipped to deal with such a problem. The difficulty lies in the fact that while the Asian and African nations which are uncommitted have no more desire than we have to see greater domination of other countries by the U.S.S.R. Having regard to the historic relations they have had with the west and having regard to their desire to flex their muscles as new and independent nations, they might think that the steps which are being taken at NATO are designed for our security, and of course they are, and they would not necessarily adopt them wholeheartedly as their measures.
We must recognize, too, that nationalism is not necessarily synonymous with communism in young countries, but we have to realize also that nationalism has been exploited by communism. There are real risks in dealing with these uncommitted nations. Their peoples may succumb to the blandishments and to the plausible and insidious appeal of soviet tactics, but we must respect them as independent nations. We must work with them and assure them that we regard them as independent nations, and try to establish a mature and wise relationship with them. Or, to put it another way, unless we assure them by word and deed that our participation in NATO is complementary to and not in conflict with our membership in the commonwealth and in the United Nations we may not be able to make much appeal to them.
Canada is a middle power with roots in the three associations, in NATO, in the commonwealth and in the United Nations. I think Canada has a special reason for avoiding an absolutely rigid dependence on any one of these organizations as the sole instrument or channel of its foreign policy.
I come now to my final point in relation to the NATO meeting projected for Paris in December. The house will not expect me- and even if it did I could not do this-to predict the specific terms of the agenda or the likely outcome of the deliberations. I am more concerned to suggest to this house the general philosophy which I think should govern our approach to that meeting. We

External Affairs
must, as I have already indicated, start from the premise that new and intensified efforts at military and scientific co-operation are essential, and we must be prepared to do our part in developing that co-operation. We must, in the second place, in view of the unhappy events of the last two or three weeks, renew our determination to consult frankly on issues which have caused, or are likely to cause, divisions in NATO. And, thirdly, to return to the point I was trying to make a few moments ago, we must assure the world outside NATO that no one need fear aggression from us; that far from regarding the forthcoming meeting as an end in itself, the whole world, including ourselves, regards it as a symbol of our determination to protect ourselves and, no less important, of our genuine and sustained interests in finding ultimate peaceful solutions to the issues that divide us from the communist world.
I have endeavoured to put before this house a diagram of Canada's relations with other nations. Nothing that I have said should obscure our intense resolution to reduce tensions between the west and the U.S.S.R. No sane person could run the risk of shutting any promising door on the possibility of co-existence. Yet-and this is not double talk-we should not fall into a propaganda plot; we should not be lulled into complacency by empty or hollow professions such as happened after the Geneva meeting. We must keep up our defences pending the arrival of the day for which we have hoped, the arrival of the day of substantial mutual trust between the west and the east. And I should add this: we must have convincing proof that the U.S.S.R. has abandoned its policies of domination. Co-existence cannot be used as a cover for subversion on the part of the U.S.S.R. in free countries. What I have been trying to say, sir, is that we must keep our powder dry and put the hand out.
Mr. Speaker, I have just been handed a message. President Eisenhower has sustained a cerebral spasm, apparently very serious. The White House now says it is a form of heart attack. That is not unrelated to what I have been trying to say.

Mr. Speaker, before I say anything else I think I will be voicing the feeling of all hon. members of this house when I express our sense of shock and regret at the news we have just heard; of the tragic misfortune which has befallen a great president of a great country, a man who has served not only his country but our own country and the world in war and in peace. We must

hope, Mr. Speaker, that this misfortune is only temporary and that the president will soon return to health and vigour. The information which I have received is to the effect that this is likely to be the case. I know we will all hope sincerely that is the case.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate my hon. friend who has just spoken, not repeating the congratulations and good wishes which I have already addressed to him in the house and outside the house, but to thank him for his comprehensive and very interesting review of the international situation as he sees it. I know that he has not been in office very long but he has already entered into the duties of that office with vigour and, I know, with the highest ideals. Perhaps I may say now what it was not possible for me to say when I occupied his position, that I am sure he is already grateful for the help and assistance he has received and will receive from the officials of the Department of External Affairs, a body of men who I think are not excelled in intelligence, devotion and industry by the foreign service of any country in the world. Perhaps I may also be permitted to thank him for his very kind words about the honour that has been recently bestowed on me because of my work in external affairs over the years.
The minister referred to his election and to the fact that he was not opposed in that by-election and expressed the hope that perhaps this would be the beginning of a habit. I must tell him that when I entered the house in a similar way in a by-election some years ago I was also not opposed by a Conservative candidate but in my case it was not the beginning of a habit and I suspect it will not be in his case either. However, we noted with interest how successful he was in what I might call a "dry run", or perhaps a "red run" would be more appropriate in this case.
In regard to what the minister has said about the necessity of maintaining good relations with other countries and in regard to the principles he laid down which would help to bring that about-and I am not going to go into this in detail-we on this side are of course in complete agreement. He did not .-and I do not criticize him for this-go into detail on some of these matters but in regard to the principles he enunciated I am sure there will be no disagreement on this side of the house.
It is a good thing for parliament to develop and maintain as much unity as is possible in such things as external affairs and as I have said more than once-and on more than one occasion I have been the beneficiary of this sentiment-however vigorously we

may disagree in this house on domestic affairs and indeed on foreign affairs when it is unavoidable, we should do our best to bring about a situation where it is possible for politics to end at the water's edge.
So far as the foreign policy of the present government is concerned, in so far as we have been able to determine it during its short period in office, there does not seem to have been very much change. I think we on this side can welcome that for the reasons which I have just indicated. But as events a year ago showed there can be division, even vigorous if not bitter division, in this house on fundamental questions of foreign policy. If I detected in some of the observations of the minister a change in attitude on some of these matters from that which I experienced in the house about a year ago perhaps that is an evidence of the chastening effect of responsibility in office. In that connection I think the minister's references to the United Nations are an example of what I have in mind. It was just about a year ago on January 22, 1957 that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), as reported at page 527 of Hansard of that date, said:
-we are making a great mistake-
The hon. member at that time was criticizing our policy at the United Nations. He said: -we are making a great mistake in placing too much reliance on this organization-
He meant the United Nations-
-for the preservation of peace.
He later added in his statement that it is the height of folly to place so much dependence on it. When he was itemizing the factors on which our foreign policy should be based he placed the United Nations at the bottom of the list at that time. The other factors mentioned by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce were the commonwealth, NATO, the United States and then the United Nations. Therefore I heard with some satisfaction the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker's) statement at the United Nations on September 23, 1957 which has been referred to and indeed this particular paragraph was quoted by my hon. friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith). The Prime Minister said:
Support of the United Nations is the cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy . . . we believe it will grow stronger-
I echo that observation.
-because it represents . . . the deep longing of mankind to strive for and attain peace and justice.
There is a relationship, I think, between this feeling that the United Nations is the cornerstone of policy and the policy which we on this side tried to bring about last
External Affairs
autumn when we were in office in connection with the Middle East. It will be, of course, very fresh in the minds of many hon. members of this house that last autumn some members of the present government when they were in opposition rejected United Nations' intervention in that dispute and attacked us very vigorously for supporting and indeed doing our best to initiate and strengthen such intervention. That Canadian policy which was based on support of the United Nations in this matter was characterized by hon. members opposite at that time as abandoning our friends. Indeed, they used stronger language than that and again I quote the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said on November 27, as reported at page 100 of Hansard:
-why in the world should we not have stood by our friends and allies . . . But no, in their hour of need we stood on the sidelines.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I did not think it was fair then to say we stood on the sidelines and I do not think it is fair now to characterize our action in those terms. We did not stand on the sidelines, but rather we did our best to support United Nations' intervention. If we at that time had followed the policy which was advocated by some hon. gentlemen opposite we would have had to vote against the intervention of the United Nations in this issue at all, and if that motion had carried and if the United Nations had not been permitted to intervene, believe me the United Nations today would not today be the cornerstone of our foreign policy.
Indeed I doubt whether the United Nations as a political organization would have been able to survive that kind of decision.
Mr. Speaker, that was one reason why I myself greeted with great pleasure the appointment of my hon. friend as Secretary of State for External Affairs. I recall how at that time he had taken what I thought was a very sound and forthright view of the Suez crisis and our policy toward it. I remember that when speaking in Quebec on April 3, 1957 to the English-speaking union in that city he said, according to the press report:
The role of Canada in the great British family of nations had been particularly noticeable and brilliant during the Middle East crisis last autumn.
He also repeated on that occasion what he said today, and I could not agree more with him, that Canada's foreign policy is not merely a reflection of the United States or of the United Kingdom. This is from the press report:
Using the Suez crisis, as an example, Dr. Smith showed that this independent policy-

External Affairs
This Canadian policy, working through the United Nations-this is my own interpolation-
-had not broken the ties and had not weakened the structure-
-of the commonwealth; I confess, of course, that when my hon. friend assumed office a little later-and we would not expect him to do otherwise-he characterized our action of a year ago in somewhat less forthright terms of approval, but he did say that he agreed in the main with what we did then. He made the qualification, however,-and I think it is an important one-that there could have been better communication within the commonwealth on this issue at that time -I agree with that, but I think it was not the fault of a Canadian government that there was no communciation at that time in regard to the Suez crisis. Perhaps at this press conference the minister might have pursued the matter a little farther but the Prime Minister interrupted him at that point.
In his statement I thought the minister made some very appropriate references to the commonwealth and to the important part it is playing in the world and the important part it should play in our development of foreign policy as well. He mentioned his own feelings when he went down to the United Nations and for the first time sat around the table with the 10 members of independent commonwealth governments from all the continents of the world except perhaps South America. I remember also-and perhaps this is an even more dramatic tribute, dramatic evidence, of the value of this association-sitting around the table with those same commonwealth members a year ago when we were not in agreement on important policy, when we were split not only two ways but three ways and four ways and yet during those difficult and indeed tragic times that friendly, fraternal association characterized by those meetings around the table persisted. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is the real test of an association, the ability to remain in friendly and intimate contact when you cannot agree on policy. Even when we do not agree on policy within the commonwealth we always try to agree, and that is the test of an association.
Perhaps I might join with my hon. friend in welcoming into this association the new independent state of Malaya. I recall how fitting were the words he used at the United Nations on the occasion of the entry of Malaya into the United Nations. That entry into the commonwealth of another Asian state, Mr. Speaker, underlines the fact that this commonwealth of nations is now in its membership predominantly Asian-African.

Of course, the core, the heart, the centre of it remains the United Kingdom, and it will always be that; but five-sixths of the population of the nations of the commonwealth are now Asian-African.
That introduces new problems of commonwealth relationships which will undoubtedly -it has already-introduce certain difficulties which have at times resulted almost in strains to our relationship. But it also gives us new opportunities inside the commonwealth, and perhaps one of the greatest and most valuable roles this association can play-and this has been said by many people before-is that it can act, it can become a bridge-it is now a bridge when there are very few bridges indeed-between Asia and the west. I join with my hon. friend in the hope that we shall do everything we can in this country to maintain and strengthen the association.
The minister also spoke of the work going on at the United Nations and I should like to congratulate him, the vice-chairman and other members of the delegation on what I think is the constructive part they have been playing down there in New York. I know a great many of the discussions, of the most difficult discussions, have centred around disarmament and I know they may have been disappointed, though they worked very hard indeed to bring about a compromise. They must have been disappointed when their efforts were not successful but only because the soviet union has refused to participate in the new committee which they and other delegations were successful in setting up. But I would not myself indulge in any great disappointment in that failure in substance because if it were not possible to work out these armaments problems in a subcommittee of five, including the four great powers, then I doubt whether a committee of 25, even with a broader composition, and including more points of view would have any greater chance of success.
I also agree with what the minister said about the effort to bring about a ban on the use of atomic and nuclear weapons. This is something that appeals to us very much indeed and must do so when we contemplate the effect of the use of those weapons on our very survival; but nevertheless it is essential, as it was considered by us when we were in office, that prohibition of that kind, to be effective and to bring about not only the ban but the confidence and trust which must go with a ban of this kind, must be surrounded by adequate provision for inspection and control. That is where the main difficulty occurs, and a difficulty which it has not yet been possible to surmount.

I would also like to join with the minister in the tribute he paid to the United Nations emergency force for the fine work it is doing in this tense and disturbed area of the world under a distinguished Canadian. Perhaps the importance of that work can be exaggerated, but nevertheless that force did bring some kind of order to a border which was in flames.
If it had not reached that area at that time and come between the opposing forces that limited conflict might have spread into something much wider, deeper and more catastrophic.
Therefore, this particular experiment, because that is all it is, has shown that the United Nations can be useful in that kind of operation. I congratulate my hon. friend for the resolution which he introduced on behalf of the Canadian delegation which would, I hope, have the effect of making this kind of thing more permanent, make it easier to set up a permanent organization and perhaps encourage the construction on those foundations of something which will be of more permanent value.
The minister then went on to talk about relations with the United States. I suppose in so far as difficulties and problems are concerned no relations between Canada and any other country-I am talking now about difficulties and complications-are as important as those with our neighbour, the United States, which, in the words of the minister, a kindly Providence has willed should be our closest neighbour. There have been occasions in the house when it has seemed to me that on some sides there has been inadequate recognition of the kindliness of Providence in putting us alongside this great neighbour. But, nevertheless, when the dust of debate clears away we are all conscious in the house of that good fortune when we compare our lot as a middle power alongside the United States, which may be a bigger power but is a partner power, with that, if you like, of a satellite communist nation alongside the Soviet union.
The minister said, I hope I am not misinterpreting what he said, that perhaps we did not make our position sufficiently clear to our neighbour when they took action which had a harmful effect on us. He went on, and I agree with him, to say that we should not be afraid to talk to them about mutual problems in a very frank and forthright way. I agree with that, Mr. Speaker, and that is one reason why I should talk this afternoon about one matter which seems to me to be not only important in our relationships with our neighbour but which might, if we are not
External Affairs
careful, lead to difficulties and complications which could be avoided. I talk about this also because there may not be any other opportunity during this session and it certainly is an important aspect of our foreign relations.
I refer to the continental air defence agreement with the United States. I am going to ask a good many questions about it because I think we are entitled to ask these questions. We have done so already in this House of Commons and I do not think that we have received answers which clear up our worries about this subject. What is this agreement? How was it reached? Well, Mr. Speaker, we do not yet know. There have been answers to questions in the house. I and members of the opposition have characterized those answers as confusing and contradictory, a characterization which has been repudiated by the Prime Minister. I think, however, it is accurate to say that the answers have not been very clarifying and that the two statements made by the Prime Minister on this subject have not added much to the clarification to which I think we are entitled.
It was complained by the Prime Minister himself, that we are pressing for secret security information. That, Mr. Speaker, is not the case, as I hope to show. But I do think that the house, and through the house the country, should be given at least as much information about this matter and the implications of it as is being given to the people of the United States by the secretary of state, Mr. Dulles. Indeed, it is in part the statements that have emanated from Washington and other places in the United States by persons in high positions of responsibility that have made it all the more necessary in our view that more information should be given here.
I do not think it is fair and I do not think it is right that responsibility in regard to this matter should be evaded by accusing us of asking for information which cannot be given on security grounds, and I do not think it is accurate to try to draw any parallel with the Ogdensburg agreement which is not the same kind of agreement at all and which was in fact tabled and discussed in the House of Commons.
The Prime Minister said the other day that we were departing from the normal course followed in the house in asking for this kind of information. I should like to quote to him from some of his previous speeches or if I cannot do that at the present time I should like merely to remind him of some of the speeches he made when on this side in regard to parliament's right to know. It has been suggested by the Prime Minister and I think

External Affairs
by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) that this North American air defence command, NORAD, is a normal development of NATO and that the arrangements regarding it were made through the United States-Canadian planning group of NATO, one of the regional groupings of NATO.
But I would point out, and there should be no misunderstanding on this score, that the NORAD air defence command or, indeed, continental defence generally-I am talking about North American continental defence generally-is not directly related to NATO at all and this particular headquarters is not a NATO command in any sense of the word. I wish it were. There is no NATO supervision or control of this organization, this agency. The regional planning group of NATO to which reference has been made is something very different indeed from a NATO command.
What we would like to have in connection with this important development in United States-Canadian relations is not any secret information about the plans which this agency may be developing or the representatives of the two defence departments may be developing. What we would like to have is information about the principles under which it is operating, the relations of the two governments concerning it and some statement which will clear up the contradictions which we think have already been made. Certainly we would expect any intergovernmental agreement, as it has been called, between the two governments of a formal, binding character to be made public but that is very different from saying that we would expect the plans under that agreement to be made public. Some of these are obviously bound to be secret and could not be made public.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what we did with the North Atlantic pact. When that was tabled, discussed and debated in the house for two or three days it was not, as the Prime Minister said the other day, primarily because it meant Canadian troops would be serving under it beyond the confines of Canada. When we discussed NATO we did not know at that time where they would be serving. In any event, if that is the main reason for bringing agreements of this kind before the House of Commons, I suppose under this agreement there will be Canadians serving outside Canada in the United States of America. Indeed, some are there already.
So far the information we have on this agreement is, as I have said, in our view confusing and contradictory. Therefore I should

like to ask a few more questions concerning it. For instance, I should like to know how much consideration was given to a plan of this importance? Was it discussed in the cabinet defence committee? How often was it discussed in full cabinet?
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, that is not a very difficult question to answer. Indeed, when the Prime Minister was talking about our own relationship to this matter, he did not hesitate to put on the record communications about cabinet discussions, as he thought they were, on this subject. They were communications which did not make it clear from whom they were or to whom they were addressed or whether or not they were cabinet documents, I am not asking what was discussed in cabinet concerning this or any other matter. I am a privy councillor. I have taken the privy councillor's oath and I know what it means.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You had better read it again.

I am trying to find out-if this matter is so important as has been indicated-how much consideration was given to it in cabinet, whether it was discussed interdepartmentally or by the cabinet defence committee before it went to the full cabinet. Surely there is no violation of the privy councillor's oath of secrecy in disclosing that kind of information. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we should not be so greatly interested in this matter now if more information had been given about it when the agreement was first announced to the press at a time when it caused a great deal of attention. I think it was last August when it was announced at a press statement, after which a press conference was held in August by the Minister of National Defence. So far as the press statement is concerned, it merely states that an agreement has been reached presumably between the two governments, to set up a system of integrated operational control of the air defence forces in the continental United States and Canada; that for

that purpose an integrated command in the United States under a United States commander was set up with a Canadian deputy, and that plans and procedures would be worked out.
When it was asked in this house: Are these plans for an integrated defence under this organization now effective, the Minister of National Defence on November 5 said "yes, on an interim basis until the formal agreement has been drawn up". But he will agree with me, I know, when I say that when this matter was first made public and when it caused so much interest no mention was made of this two-stage procedure. Therefore what is the nature of this interim agreement between our two countries, on such an important matter, under which this headquarters is now operating? What is the formal agreement contemplated to which reference has already been made? Can everything be done under this interim agreement which is contemplated under the formal agreement?
At the August press conference to which I have referred the minister, dealing with some of these questions, said that the integrated headquarters would develop plans and procedures required for the tremendously rapid decisions which will have to be taken. There is no doubt that in an emergency they will have to be taken rapidly but they will be taken by whom? At a press conference the minister said, and I quote from a record made at that conference:
I think that the commander (who would be an American) or in his absence the deputy commander will decide on the proper action.
That is a quotation from a record made at the press conference. Then, as he is reported, he went on to say this and I quote again from this record:
It is a matter of seconds-there is no time for consultation. If war comes they will put their agreed-on plans into effect.
Does that mean, Mr. Speaker, that this can be done and the decisions to which reference has been made therefore taken only "if war comes"?
The minister appeared to answer his own question, and this is where some of our confusion began when, according to this report, he added that the joint operational control will become effective "as soon as a group of planes has been determined to be hostile". That means that that decision might have to be taken-and I certainly agree with this- before war comes.
