Therefore, in the light of this press conference and in the light of the statement made at that time, surely hon. members opposite should not have been surprised when we had some questions to ask
External Affairs
about this matter on the assembly of parliament. What about the answer to those questions in parliament in clearing up some of these ambiguities of the earlier questions and answers? On November 5, in answer to a question-and I may say that I am quoting from page 758 of Hansard-the Minister of National Defence said this:
-the arrangements for setting up this command-
That is NORAD.
-followed a similar pattern to those governing our forces serving with the supreme allied command in Europe and the naval forces in the Atlantic under the supreme allied commander, Atlantic . . . and followed closely the procedure which had been set up during the Mackenzie-President Roosevelt conversations before the last war . . . for the mutual defence of this continent.
I contend, Mr. Speaker-and I have already said this-that there really is no basis for that kind of parallel at all between those two situations. The NATO treaty was debated in this house for days and the Ogdens-burg agreement was also discussed before the house. Yet on the same day the Minister of National Defence, in answer to another question, seemed to me to contradict his own statement at the press conference of August. As reported at page 758 of Hansard he said this:
In the event of a national emergency occurring General Partridge,-
That is the United States commander.
-after consultation with the Canadian and United States governments, would be able to commit either American or Canadian forces in the defence of this country.
Naturally, after his having said that, we asked him how would consultation take place and he replied the next day "by telephone or other means". The Globe and Mail next day characterized that reply as "arrant and dangerous nonsense". The Winnipeg Tribune put it in this way, "Slogan should be shoot now, telephone later".
General Partridge himself had said, however, on September 6, that he did not have to obtain first the permission even of the president of the United States or to wire Washington in an emergency. The secretary of state, Mr. Dulles, on November 20-and this is more recent evidence-said this, according to the press report of his statement:
If an attack were made on NATO forces the decision to shoot would be made by the commander on the spot.
If this command is not a NATO one, nevertheless American and Canadian forces presumably defending our own continent are NATO forces.
Then to come back to the minister's reply in the House of Commons on November 7, it seemed to me that he really had watered

External Affairs
down this command to a purely planning agency, and emphasized quite rightly that the decision to go to war must always rest with the government. No other interpretation would be tolerable. But that does not, oi course, answer the question. What about the decision to put planes into action? Does that await a declaration of war? If not, who makes the necessary decision? Also, if this command is merely a planning group, then why all the fuss about it? Why make so much of it? Why make so much of it and why make this announcement about it in July and August under an interim arrangement? Why not wait until parliament met in October when we could have learned all about it?
It seems to me that the crux of the correct Canadian position could be put into a single sentence: If General Partridge and the air defence command of the United States have any authority over Canadian forces they should have it as officers responsible not only to the United States but also to Canada. That is the situation in Paris at the present time and it has worked very well there in the NATO command. If, as may be assumed, General Partridge has to secure the authority of the president before he launches into the air the forces under his command-unless an attack has already begun-and those forces include Canadian forces, then surely he must also have authority from the government of Canada.
If this is to be included in any intergovernmental agreement we would like to know about it. If authorization is to be given in advance to act under certain conditions, which may well be necessary in the circumstances under which we live today, then those conditions must be clearly defined and agreed to by Canada as well as the United States, through its constitutional authorities acting in accordance with constitutional practice. Yet, from the answers we have received, it is very difficult indeed to find out just what is the situation.
Now it is not a question of approving or disapproving the setting up of a continental command; how can we approve or disapprove of such a thing when we really do not yet know anything about it. It is not a question of giving up or hanging on to sovereignty. We have previously acted in ways which involve the abdication, in the interests of our security, of some of our sovereignty. Perhaps rather than using the word abdication I should say we have made our sovereignty work for our security and that is the only way a country can guarantee its security in these times. We have shown this by our participation in the European forces

of NATO and I am sure we would be glad to do the same thing in respect of our participation in continental defence if it is found necessary to work in that way after discussion and approval by this house.
Now that I have mentioned NATO, I would like to say something about this organization which, in my opinion, remains indispensable to our policy of collective security. I was very glad to hear what the hon. minister had to say about the approach of the government and himself to NATO. He indicated, and I certainly agree with him, that it is regrettable that in NATO we seem to act	only	after	we have	received	someshock	from	those	who,	in	a sense,	were
responsible for NATO in the first place.
This	has	been	very	dramatically	demonstrated in our reaction to the launching by the soviet union of the satellites. That indeed	was	a surprise	and	a shock, but
perhaps it should not have been so much of a surprise to us. If we had been aware of what was going on in the soviet union, it certainly would not have been. However, the reaction which has taken place as a result of this shock, so far as NATO is concerned, has I think been a healthy one. It has underlined the necessity of a stronger and more unified organization; it has I think also emphasized the necessity of a stronger and more imaginative diplomacy. In that regard perhaps we would do well, without minimizing the importance of the United Nations as a great forum for the discussion and hammering out of international problems on a world basis, to pay greater attention to the resources and effectiveness of well-tried and normal channels of diplomacy, as we face these new problems.
I was reading in the New York Times just the other day a review of an article by a distinguished American and former ambassador, Mr. John C. Wiley. He said, and this is worthy of attention today:
Today it is of vital importance to edge, if possible, the grave issues of the moment back into normal diplomatic channels . . . Perhaps only a meeting in the valley, a meeting on the working level, could begin to disentangle the tortured skein ... a meeting under the tyranny neither of clock nor calendar.
If I emphasize, as I believe my hon. friend emphasized, the necessity of pursuing that kind of diplomacy vigorously and effectively in our desire to try to solve, one by one and step by step, the problems which now divide the world, that does not mean that we need to weaken in any way shape or form either our collective defence or our collective action in NATO. So far as closer co-operation and unity in NATO are concerned, I welcome and I am sure all members of the

official opposition welcome this meeting to take place at the summit in December and I hope that as a result of that meeting some steps will be taken to bring about the closer unity which we, when we were in government along with our friends in NATO, were not able to make effective.
I know how big the problem is; I know how when there is a shock everybody talks about unity and when we recover from the shock we go back to our old ways of doing things individually. Certainly the problem is not a simple one and to solve it we will have to use NATO more as an agent for consultation and co-operation than we have done in the past.
Mr. Spaak, the very energetic and able secretary general of NATO put it this way, and I cannot think of any better text for the next meeting of the NATO council than this speech which he gave in Bruges during September of last year. Said Mr. Spaak:
It remains to be seen now whether one can start a discussion amongst the members of the Atlantic community, a real preliminary consultation which is really loyal and really complete, that is to say, before the individual governments have come to final decisions. I must tell you frankly that the success of this stage is essential to the survival of the Atlantic alliance and I do think that if we do not succeed in achieving that, and if in its day to day political life the large countries of the alliance did not, with their lesser allies, succeed in finding common ground upon which they could take up unchallenged positions and defend them together, but if on the contrary they continue to make difficulties for one another, I am quite certain that the alliance would crumble, with the consequences that I have indicated.
Now that was the secretary general of NATO speaking, a man who is not given to pessimism. It was only a year ago that a report dealing with this very subject, the strengthening of consultation and co-operation within NATO in the non-military field, was made to the NATO council by a committee of three. In making that report we were not working under the influence of a shock such as we are doing today. A year ago, when that report was discussed, everybody agreed with it and, so far as I know -and I admit perhaps I do not know all about it-the report was then pigeonholed and little or nothing has been done to implement the recommendations.
That report, for instance, recommended among other things an exchange of information on scientific and technical matters. Indeed, it recommended the calling together of a scientific and technical NATO conference. That proposal, when it was made, did not attract very much attention but I am glad to note it is being taken up now by those who are in a position to put it into effect. And when we discussed this question of consultation about a year ago, everybody
External Affairs
was in favour of it in principle, but at the same time the more powerful members of NATO soon let it be known, as indeed they are beginning to let it be known now as the day for this summit meeting comes closer, that consultation is a wonderful thing in NATO but that it must not be carried out in such a way as to interfere inappropriately with the prior requirement of consultation within a government, and that it must not be allowed to interfere with the requirement for quick national action. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is far less danger of that happening than there is that these reasons will be used to prevent consultation being carried out in NATO beforehand, not after events had taken place.
We have had a very good example how not to proceed in this regard in the recent case of arms shipments to Tunisia. I know how difficult and complicated this problem can be and I know it impinges on a great many areas of policy, but surely it could have been discussed confidentially beforehand. The NATO council might have had a part to play before the disagreement between the three powers concerned became public. Perhaps if the question had been discussed inside the council this type of public disagreement which has come, to say the least at a very unfortunate time, might have been avoided.
NATO, then, remains the foundation of our policy for collective security. But behind NATO and more important even than NATO is the necessity for the negotiation of problems which divide the two worlds, as and when opportunity affords or may be created for that purpose. Therefore I should like to end on this note: while we must, as the minister said, remain strong in our defence, we must also remain strong and imaginative in our diplomacy, and we must work together, in NATO and elsewhere, not only to be strong but so that we can solve the problems which lie behind the division of the world, whose solution, if one can be found, would perhaps make it unnecessary for us to be so strong in a military sense that we in this country today have to divert about 40 per cent of our revenue to defence.
Mr. M. J. Cold well (Roseiown-Biggar): Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with other hon. members who have spoken in expressing the concern we all feel about the condition of the President of the United States. We know this creates a great problem for the American people because, unlike our own constitution, there is no settled way of dealing with business when the president is incapacitated.

External Affairs
Should a president die, there is, of course, a vice-president to act in his place, but I understand that incapacity is not provided for, and therefore I wish to join with others in expressing our sincere concern about the position of the United States.
I should like also to congratulate the minister on the assumption of his new duties in the government of Canada and in the House of Commons. I was hoping this afternoon that as a new minister in a new government he might have laid before the house a comprehensive statement of the policies of the government with regard to international affairs along more general lines than he did, but we will look forward to his doing this on a future occasion.
I must tell the bon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) that I did sympathize with him when he was "needling" the government a bit about its attitude a year ago at the time of the Suez crisis, and citing the minister for external affairs in support of the position taken by many of us in this house at that time. I do not think any of us were asleep when we read about the introduction of the minister when he arrived at Ottawa by air and was asked a question about Suez, to which he was proceeding to reply when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) intervened rather hurriedly to say that of course the minister's policy is consonant with that of the government of the day. Hon. members who had taken a different view from those who are now members of the government with regard to the Suez crisis were not slow to notice this incident.
I was glad to hear the minister say that Canada would continue to press for measures of disarmament and methods of reaching agreement in that field. The minister said that he and his colleagues would continue to press for disarmament, and I think it is right Canada should do so because it is obvious that the time has come when national armaments can no longer guarantee the safety and security of any country.
At this time we are witnessing a desperate and dangerous arms race between two of the great powers. I say only two great powers because there are only two great powers, Russia and the United States. They alone remain great in terms of power. These two nations, and the other nations which by domination or alliance are associated with them, have failed to reach any agreement on how we might eliminate the threat of war. All nations engaged in this arms race must eventually face drastic reductions in their standard of living and social services. The President of the United States has warned

his people to this effect while demanding still greater appropriations for scientific development of new and terrible weapons of war.
Canadians who were hopeful of reductions in defence expenditures are being warned that instead of money being diverted from defence we may find we may have to expend more in producing scientific instruments of war. That, of course, would prevent the diversion we should like to see, namely aid to underprivileged nations which I think is essential for the welfare and peace of the world.
I said that discussions among the great powers had failed to reach agreements. Their discussions have filled mankind with anxiety because since the war their diplomacy has degenerated into insults and threats. As the days pass their insults become more direct and their threats more violent. As their weapons become more terrible, mutual fear of ultimate destruction overshadows ordinary people everywhere.
The time has come when this parliament of Canada should take a new look at both our foreign policy and our defence commitments. Recent developments in international affairs have filled thoughtful Canadians not only with anxiety but with understandable apprehension; apprehension not so much of threats of war from any potential enemy, but indeed fear that the policies we, with others, have followed in recent years are fraught with danger to our own country and to the peace of the world.
The nations assembled at the San Francisco conference in 1945 and the delegates who comprised the delegations there together with the populations behind them believed that the charter of the United Nations provided an effective means of preventing another world war. Of course, it should be said that in spite of recurrent threats of war the United Nations has provided a forum where disputes could be aired and where means could be taken to stop minor acts of aggression which might lead to the outbreak of war among the great powers. May I say immediately that this justifies our support of the United Nations and indeed makes it essential that the United Nations shall be the cornerstone of our external policy.
The instrument for the prevention of aggression approved in the charter was never brought into being. The military staffs of the five principal powers have never established the international security or police force that was to function under the direction of the security council of the United Nations. Because of this, last year largely because of the proposals made by Canada, the United Nations

assembly created an emergency force to prevent the continuance of war in the Middle East and ordered the withdrawal of British, French and Israeli troops from Egypt. I want to say immediately that to their credit the order was obeyed promptly. While no similar action with regard to a force was taken to ensure the ending of the Russian aggression and the withdrawal of soviet troops from Hungary a similar order was ignored by the soviets. The action taken in the Middle East however showed that some advance had been made in the prevention of war by United Nations action.
We believe that Canada should give leadership in the cause of world peace and security by urging the United Nations assembly not only to maintain this security force but to urge the establishment of an expanded international police force designed to maintain international law and order. The great powers having failed to fulfil their function the assembly must assume the responsibility of maintaining law and order among the nations and if this requires amendment to the charter of the United Nations we should press for that amendment. Canada is not one of the so-called great powers but from time to time nations with populations many times our own have looked to us as a nation with no ulterior aim, without colonial ambitions and with no desire to dominate anyone else for the leadership which I think at times we have failed to give.
The common people of all nations without exception cry aloud for deliverance from ever pressing fears and for peace in our time and in the years beyond our time. The C.C.F. believes that this parliament at this time should seek a new approach in external affairs to match today's scientific developments to cope with the social and economic problems that confront the world. That is what I meant when I said at the outset that I had hoped with a new government and a new minister we might have had something more specific regarding our international policy than we received this afternoon.
The great powers having failed to find such an approach we believe that the lesser powers, if I may term them as such-the smaller and middle nations-should assume the responsibility of demanding the elimination of the dreadful threat of nuclear war and that we should associate ourselves with and give leadership to the smaller and middle nations in pressing this point home. We believe further that because of the confidence that has been shown in Canada from time to time by many nations this government
External Affairs
should take immediate steps to accept leadership and to play a more significant role in mankind's efforts to establish peace on a firm and lasting foundation.
Now, you ask how this can be done. In the first place-and here I agree with the former minister of external affairs-whenever a proposal is made by one or other of the great powers which seems even remotely to offer an opportunity for negotiation Canada should be ready to advise and to press for acceptance, should be prepared to assist in arrangements and, when possible and proper, should be prepared to join with other nations in such negotiations.
Very recently the Russian leader Khrushchev made a public pledge never to start a war. At the same time he proposed a new high level conference with representatives of capitalist states to ban war, to end the armament race, to achieve co-existence and the settlement of ideological differences through peaceful competition for the development of economics, culture and the better satisfaction of man's needs. Now, what was the immediate reaction? The immediate reaction from Washington was that this was another propaganda move and should be ignored. Canada accepted that opinion as did other nations which followed the United States lead. Yet, Mr. Speaker, was it not possible that the Soviet union, having recently demonstrated her strength through remarkable scientific advances, was making a new and this time perhaps a genuine attempt to bring about some easement in the cold war?
We know they have achieved leadership in the production of guided missiles and altogether likely in thermonuclear weapons. They are well aware that their country is surrounded by air bases manned so the newspapers tell us-not only the newspapers but the officials of the United States-with many hundreds of jet bombers equipped and ready with unbelievably destructive warheads. They know that an attack on North America, an attack on any part of Europe or elsewhere would be met by equally devastating attacks immediately on Russian industrial centres and populations.
I ask you if it is not remotely possible, therefore, that a new approach to peaceful negotiations might offer some success? Can we go along with the President of the United States who, in the first series of broadcasts discussing the earth satellite described the Soviet union-1 listened to him carefully- not as a rival in the scientific process but rather as "the enemy", as though his nation were at war. It is true that frightening statements have been made from time to time by soviet leaders but certainly frightening

External Affairs
statements have also been made by Mr. John Foster Dulles of the United States as well as by many other leaders in that country.
Where will all this lead us but eventually to war, a war in which there would be no victors, only victims; a war of mutual suicide? We do not believe that Canada should sit idly by and tolerate this drift toward disaster. This parliament and this government should demand that a new look be taken not only at our external policies but those of our Department of National Defence for defence and foreign policy are inextricably mixed up together.
We of the C.C.F. have supported measures that were in the previous stage of international affairs, we believe, designed to protect our people and indeed our friends from unprovoked attack. That seemed reasonable and proper but we know now that neither we in North America nor the people of Russia can find security in early warning radar lines, jet fighters or nuclear warheads on our guns. The only road to peace and security, it appears to us, surely now lies in promoting understanding and by negotiation arriving at mutual agreements to live and let live.
Our government should make it abundantly clear that we will support no policy or diplomacy of threats of studied insults, of abusive language in international affairs which may end in war. This we should make known both to the Soviet union and to the United States. Over the years I have been at the United Nations, I have heard the Soviet leaders indulge in insulting and abusive language. And, if I may mention him again, I think it should be made known particularly to Mr. John Foster Dulles whose meanderings around the world making provocative speeches everywhere fill intelligent people with alarm.
It is time then that Canada followed an external policy consonant with our international interests and our international reputation. We have not always done that, as witness our policy regarding China. Throughout history and indeed under international precedent nations recognize revolutionary governments when they obviously control a nation. Our own history is replete with examples. Nations had to recognize the British revolution of 1689, still celebrated in many parts of Canada on July 12 and the American revolution of 1776 when the forbears of many Canadians suffered grievously because they resisted it.
We remember the terror of the French revolution of 1789 and the bolshevik revolution of 1917; but the world finally recognized

the facts of the new revolutionary governments, that they ruled the nations involved. Why then should recognition be withheld from 600 million people in China proper when such a policy has driven them closer to the Soviet union, a nation which the President of the United States characterized earlier this month as the enemy? I believe it is because Washington would frown upon our doing so.
The Chinese, like the Russians, are on the march. Soon we may discover that the stories we have heard of their backwardness, their illiteracy, their ignorance, will be in the same category as stories told until very recently about the Russians. Perhaps, too, many of us were brought up in childhood, as I was brought up, to believe that the Chinese were heathen Chinese, people who were on a lower level than ourselves. We know that that is not true and never has been true.
So long were our people fed propaganda about Russia, to which I have alluded, that when journalists like I. Norman Smith, bankers like James Muir, businessmen like James Duncan, told us of the educational, industrial and scientific progress of Russia, what was said of them? They were characterized as dupes of communist propaganda.
Now, many of us, of course, knew that while there was widespread illiteracy, poverty and disease in China, there were also many thousands of highly cultured Chinese who were heirs of an ancient and historically peaceful culture which even revolution could not destroy.
They were not in sympathy with the Chinese government.
You don't believe in that.

As a matter of fact, I am stating a historical fact. If the minister understands the history of Asia he will know that the Chinese throughout their history have had leaders who were highly cultured and who were peaceful in their intent.

On a point of personal explanation, may I say to the hon. leader of the C.C.F. that I was not questioning the intelligence of a large group of independent people in China but I said they were not in sympathy with the Chinese government.
How do you know that?
Well, I know.

As a matter of fact, many of us were not ignorant of the fact that the Chinese revolution against a corrupt regime was led in part at least by scholars in their

universities, joined by thousands of university students. In other words, in the leadership, among others, were Chinese intellectuals.
The European situation was commented upon as lately as Sunday by Mr. George F. Kennan, the former United States ambassador to Moscow, who is now lecturing at Oxford University. He was speaking over the British Broadcasting Corporation network. He urged in a radio address from London that the western nations make a re-appraisal of their policies, leading to the possible withdrawal of both eastern and western troops from Germany. I found considerable satisfaction myself in his remarks because, speaking in Montreal on December 14, 1956, I advocated a similar policy and I should like to quote what I had to say on that occasion. I was criticized for it. I said:
The west should be prepared to make imaginative and far-reaching proposals that will, by diplomatic means, achieve the freedom of the peoples of eastern Europe.
I was talking mainly about the Soviet aggression in Hungary. I said:
We cannot intervene militarily but we can make a bold attempt by other means to obtain the right of these states to determine their own destiny. Canada should take the lead in urging that the western nations offer to withdraw all foreign troops from Europe in return for the withdrawal of all Russian troops from eastern Europe and for the establishment of a guaranteed neutral zone between the U.S.S.R. and the western European powers. It would be best if the whole operation were conducted and guarantees given under a United Nations auspices. There may very well be some prospects of success in this suggestion if the west has the imagination to make it in a constructive way.
Consequently, I was very interested indeed in reading what the former United States ambassador to Moscow had to say, a man who cannot be charged with friendliness to the communist regime during the time that he occupied that important position in the Soviet union. One appeals to governments to act; but if governments will not act to achieve peace by negotiation and otherwise to remove the threats of war, does any other approach offer any hope for the easing of tensions and the imminent threat of war? I think there are other channels.
The C.C.F. believes at least that there are channels open to us to approach the soviet people. I was happy to view the hockey match last Friday evening between the team from Whitby, representing Canada, and the Russian team. The huge crowd in Maple Leaf Gardens at Toronto were obviously friendly to the visitors. The players showed every sign of good will and sportsmanship in victory and in defeat. Such events here and in Russia can exert an influence for good. I hope there will be more of them. It confirms our opinion that
External Affairs
the ordinary people of all countries are just people who want to live in peace with their neighbours.
I think another and much more important channel is the subject of editorial comment in the New York Herald Tribune of November 8, and has been, I may add, the subject of editorial comment in some of our own Canadian papers in more recent days.
The Herald Tribune, republican in sympathy, conservative in outlook, cannot be accused of communistic sympathies. The editors drew attention to a special bulletin sent out by the editor of the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists of the United States, a most important and interesting periodical. Ever since it was first published I have subscribed to it.
This special bulletin contained a communication from 155 leading Soviet scientists, together with a formal resolution by the presidium of the academy of sciences of the U.S.S.R. The communication itself was signed by six of the soviet's outstanding scientists, including the world famous physicist, Peter Kapitsa, a graduate of Cambridge University whose laboratory was moved to Russia and established there with the assistance and cooperation of the English university's most eminent nuclear scientists some 25 years ago. Kapitsa is said to be the scientist responsible for the satellite. The resolution proposed a broad international conference of scientists to discuss the dangers to mankind of a thermonuclear war. I am going to read the letter, It is in these words:
Let not only atomic scientists of all countries but also representatives of other disciplines, biologists, medical scientists, philosophers of all schools, economists, historians, sociologists, educators, etc., express their weighty opinions in a broad international meeting of the most important representatives of science. In such a tense time, full of danger of a general destructive war, scientists cannot remain aside. Their duty is to add their voice to the requests for the cessation of atomic tests. The danger which hangs over mankind because of the possibility of using atomic energy for war purposes is common to all countries independent of their political and economic systems.
We the soviet scientists express our full readiness for common effort with scientists of any other country, to discuss any proposals directed towards the prevention of atomic war, the creation of secure peace, and tranquility for all mankind.
The editor of the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists comments that while the letter repeats some communist propaganda demands, the writers recognize the necessity of avoiding atomic wars rather than merely that of abolishing atomic weapons, a very significant difference in approach. The editor urged scientists of the west to take up this offer.
The Herald Tribune then pointed out that this soviet offer grew from a conference on a

External Affairs
smaller scale held in Canada last summer at the summer home of Mr. Cyrus Eaton at Pugwash, Nova Scotia. On the same page of the newspaper Mr. Cyrus Eaton had an article warmly approving of the suggestion and naming Canada as one suitable location for the conference.
Of course I realize that this appeal, as the Prime Minister said when I drew it to his attention, was not on a governmental level, but I see no reason why our government should not encourage our scientists to invite such a conference to Canada and assist them in every way to make it a success. On the contrary, I see every reason why our government should do so.
Here surely is a new channel of approach by men and women whose activities are based on scientific knowledge which is international. A few years ago some people were prone to refer to scientists and philosophers as "eggheads". Today who will deny that the future of the world rests with such people rather than some irresponsible politicians-
You are one of them.

-some rather open-mouthed generals and admirals and some backbenchers who have made and are making a sorry mess of their opportunities and their responsibilities.
In 1945 some politicians in the United States made the mistake of believing that the mathematics at the root of scientific advances could be the secret of their country. Future historians may regard this erroneous opinion as one of the important roots of the distrust and misunderstandings that have plagued the world in the past decade. They refused to allow their knowledge to be shared with their allies, even some who had provided them with the very basis of the atomic discovery they determined to keep to themselves, and principally among these, of course, were their British and Canadian allies.
I might add that Mr. Eaton pointed out in the article to which I have referred that the men who produced the first atomic bomb were not all Americans. They were Italians, Danes, Poles and Germans as well, I may add, as British, French, Canadians and others. Of the proposed scientific conference suggested in the Herald Tribune Mr. Eaton had this to say:
It is certainly something that colleges and universities can back. Certainly anyone who is a capitalist ought to go for it because in a war all the material accumulations of the past would go. One hydrogen bomb would lay this great city (New York) in rubble.

Surely capitalists, socialists and, yes, communists, share this common dread and should seek a common way out of the danger that overhangs the world.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, there is
another aspect of this problem which deserves more consideration by this house than it has received in the past. In the end, war or no war, annihilation or not for many millions, the most potent urge among mankind will remain "hunger" and hunger today is widespread across the world.
As a vital part of our external policy, the government should be supporting more completely and more generously every intelligent proposal for economic and technical aid. We should not gear our support to that of any nation, as we have been doing. Canada has said that because certain nations pay certain fractions of funds for technical aid, we are prepared to contribute only what we consider to be the proportionate fraction too. The United Nations assembly is again debating the special United Nations fund for economic development which has been before the assembly for several years and which is designed to provide capital grants and loans to the underdeveloped countries of Asia and Africa, under the auspices of the United Nations. Canada has joined the United States and the United Kingdom in opposing this project both before the economic and social council and the appropriate committee of the United Nations. This fund is designed to plan capital assistance with political and profit considerations giving way to human need.
May I say that this afternoon I was disappointed that the minister did not accept the suggestion made by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Macdonald) and give a more hopeful answer to his question.
In the vote about to be taken at the assembly Canada should assert its moral leadership among the nations that want to support this fund in spite of the opposition of the United States delegation. Apart from this, we should be prepared to make further and large appropriations for the Colombo plan. The increase in the Colombo plan proposed by the government at this session is paltry in comparison with the needs of southeast Asia, in particular India, and our

own gross national production, as are the other contributions mentioned this afternoon by the minister in his address to the house. We should divert at least one-quarter of the amount this parliament is providing in our defence appropriations to SUNFED, technical aid, the Colombo plan and other international humanitarian efforts. Other nations should do the same so that disease and hunger could be banished from the world in a relatively short time. That would do more to remove the threats of world-wide dictatorships of the communist or fascist varieties than all the stockpiles of atomic warheads and guided missiles the western nations could conceivably acquire.
When we come to a discussion of the government's defence proposals we shall have more to say about this aspect of our defence expenditures. Suffice it now to say that we look forward to and must work for the day when Canada can abandon armaments entirely for offence as well as defence all across the world.
To sum up, then, we state categorically that we are not satisfied with our external affairs policies. They do not meet the needs of the country in this period of danger from new and terrible weapons that modern war would loose upon mankind. We therefore take this opportunity of urging this house and this government to adopt a new approach to the problem that besets us. There must be an end to a diplomacy based on threats and insults. Canada, which has been comparatively free from this type of diplomacy, should denounce it whenever it is indulged in and whoever indulges in it.
Our approach to international problems must be devised to meet today's scientific developments and to cope with the social and economic problems of the nations and the peoples of the world, regardless of race, creed, colour or ideology. We should thus give every encouragement and support to plans and financial contributions for the relief of hunger and disease among the less privileged peoples of the world as well as, indeed, within our own borders. Hence, because the United Nations does offer and afford opportunities to exercise such leadership, we must continue to support and to enhance the prestige of the United Nations.
We believe that Russia and the United States both must know that either they will meet to achieve a settlement of political differences between them or, sooner or later, mutual suicide will result. Canada's role now should be to give a definite and imaginative lead, to the middle and smaller nations at least, to demand that negotiations between the two great powers and their allies should be undertaken on every possible occasion.
External Affairs
Today, because of the anxieties we all feel, there is at least a possibility that such leadership offered by Canada might meet with a large measure of success since the peoples of all nations share our fear that a continuance of the present nuclear arms race can have no other end than universal destruction for us all. We want the world to heed the message which in less than a month will ring out once more across the world as it has for centuries in the past among the Christian nations of the world: "Peace on earth, good will to men".

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I should first of all like to associate the members of this group with the expressions of regret and sympathy we all felt when we heard that the President of the United States had been stricken. It is our sincere hope and prayer that he may speedily be restored to his usual health.
I should also like to extend congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) as he takes over the portfolio of this extremely important department. We welcome the opportunity that is presented at this time to discuss the world picture in general and Canada's position within that picture in particular. I regret very much, Mr. Speaker, that the time for this debate is so limited. I should like to remind the house that more time was spent yesterday in debating the advisability of setting up a committee to consider the installation of a translation system than has been allowed today for the debating of our position in international affairs. I am not in any way minimizing the importance of the debate of yesterday. However, in view of the tremendous factors involved in the debate today, I feel that much longer than one day should have been set aside for this important discussion.
I should like to thank the secretary of state for his report this afternoon, for it was a report dealing with the activities of the Canadian delegation at the United Nations and also the contribution Canada is making in respect of a number of other phases of our international policy and program.
I should like also to say that we would have welcomed a direct statement of policy on the part of the minister and the government at this time in order to help us get a grasp and an understanding of the direction in which this government proposes to lead Canada in relation to our external affairs. Of course, I think it has been fairly definitely stated that there would be no fundamental change in policy. We therefore can only assume that the direction that was followed

External Affairs
by the previous government will to a large extent be followed by the present government.
Reference was made today to the NATO organization. Right at the outset-and I do not propose to spend very much time tonight on these individual organizations-I should like to say that we are in complete agreement with the objective of the NATO organization. In view of the inability of the United Nations to cope with the problem and in order to place us in a position where we can defend ourselves and maintain our own security, we feel it was necessary to set up a separate organization such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; and today, as never before, we are impressed with the necessity of maintaining this organization and perhaps strengthening it but certainly in no wise minimizing its importance.
When I state our support of this organization I should like to say as well that we believe that a clear statement should be made, and reiterated time and time again, that NATO is a defensive organization, and a defensive organization only, with no plans for aggression, with no designs upon other nations, and that it is there solely as an instrument to effect and maintain our security.
Reference has been made to the Colombo plan and of course we in this group have always given our wholehearted support to the principle underlying the Colombo plan and the expanding program for technical assistance of the United Nations. We have always felt, as we still feel, that the contributions made by Canada to these organizations are an investment; they are not a handout or just a contribution given to ease our conscience in view of world need, but an investment whereby we contribute to the betterment of the world, enabling the underprivileged to assist themselves, to raise their standards of living and to place themselves on a much higher plane than that on which they are existing at the present time from economic and social points of view.
Now since we last discussed foreign affairs events have moved with incredible speed and we now find ourselves being directed away from our role as earthbound peoples into the realm of space and inter-planetary travel, with all the exhilarating or catastrophic possibilities which these ventures may produce. At least to the ordinary citizen of Canada, the achievement of soviet scientific knowledge and skill has caused an impact that will not soon be forgotten. We had imagined that the United States and Britain were so far advanced in these scientific and engineering fields that no other nation could possibly eclipse them, but what we have heard and

read during these past few weeks has disillusioned us and we are asking "Now what?"
I am sure we all remember the forebodings and the fears consequent upon the dropping of the A-bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. We were on that occasion ushered very unceremoniously into a new age but it was an age of fear besides being an age of wonder. Following that circumstance we heard the dire predictions that the end of the world was really in view and may I remind hon. members that these predictions were not made by some so-called wild-eyed preachers of doom but by scientists, legislators and statesmen the free world over. Perhaps it could be that we were at that time arriving at the point referred to in the scriptures when men's hearts were failing for fear of those things which were coming to pass upon the earth. Now, upon the minds of men, already taut with the remembrance of those things to which I have referred, there comes the terrific impact and realization of new and even greater inventions, the fearsome or the beneficial results of which are still clouded in the mists of uncertainty.
Now what is the significance of this great new advance in modern science? What does it mean to us that this invention is first of all in the hands of a power constituting possibly the greatest and only threat to our free way of life? These are important questions. However, we find that fear in many instances in the past has provided an incentive for action in other fields of endeavour and so the fear of this new advance in science by the soviet union has had the effect of shaking those in the western world out of their complacency.
I ask this question: Why did this thing come as such a surprise to us? How was it possible that these achievements could be reached without any intimation being gained or received by the western world that such things were in the offing? Was it because we had been lulled into a false sense of security; was it because we had somehow settled back and under perhaps the relaxation of certain tensions had forgotten the tremendous possibilities that existed in other parts of the world? Why was it that this thing had to come with such an element of surprise?
Perhaps the former government could give some answer to that question, but granted that this thing which has been invented could be of inestimable value from a purely scientific point of view-and we are reminded that the soviet union has promised to share the data and information obtained with the rest of the world-I do not think we can get away from the conviction that its value

from the military standpoint is far beyond the present conception of most individuals and, in the hands of a great and unfriendly power, could have disastrous consequences for the free world.
Without question it was the realization of this fact that threw American military and scientific brains into an all-out effort, not only to close the gap, but to again take the lead in this all-important field. President Eisenhower ordered full speed ahead, and then, in consultation with the leaders of our other friendly powers has urged the consolidation of the free nations of the world into a unified force to defeat the worldwide designs of the communist leaders.
Now it is against this backdrop that we pause to take our bearings today and to discover, if we can, just where we as a nation fit into the international picture; to try and discover, if we can, whether or not our foreign policy is designed to accomplish the greatest good for ourselves and for other parts of the world. That is why we would have welcomed today a more direct statement of policy on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We ask the question: What is involved in the marshalling of the united forces of the free world into a unit or instrument capable of defeating the aggressive designs of the soviet? First of all I suppose it comes to our minds that this involves the pooling of our military power and potential.
For some years now we have been engaged in a feverish race for military superiority. Canada's contribution to this end has cost us in the neighbourhood of $2 billion per year and although I am sure Canadians right across the country are prepared to make every sacrifice necessary to preserve our way of life and freedom, yet the question is becoming increasingly persistent: Just where are we going? What is to be the final outcome of all our feverish activities? I do not have to take the time tonight to refer to the tremendous military build-up of the past few years the arms race where each nation was trying to outdo the other, not only in manpower but in fighting power in armaments of all descriptions. Think of the cost to the nations. We see that with all our expenditure and with all our efforts and all the application of our skills and powers, when we reach a certain plateau we still have further expenditures before us and greater sacrifices than ever before. So the question is: where does it end?
They tell us that before one aircraft is in production it is obsolescent and they are already working on something new. There
External Affairs
was a tremendous expenditure for something, but we did not know whether or not it was going to be brought into use. And yet because we could not wait for the ultimate in weapons I suppose we had to fill in the gap with these other things. The struggle, it seems to me, still goes on.
I remember well back in 1954 when it was my privilege to attend the United Nations session as an observer, debates were then going on relative to disarmament, and it seems to me I spent most of my time sitting in that committee listening to speech after speech, debate after debate, trying to find some common ground, some common meeting place of opinion. But it seemed to end in frustration. And so, year after year, it goes on, and it does not seem that we are getting any closer to the answer to the problem; it does not seem as if we are reaching a solution.
And now, as outlined today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we find that seemingly the matter has reached a stalemate, that the Soviet union refuses to participate any further in the deliberations on disarmament. However, we must continue to press on; we must continue to seek a solution; we must endeavour to find an answer to the riddle which has proved so perplexing down through the years.
But, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the futility of armaments as an effective system for the building of the kind of world we envisage for ourselves and for succeeding generations. What kind of world do we want? If we want a world where men can live without fear, if we want a world free from want, if we want a world where an opportunity is given for the full development of human prosperity, then all our military endeavours, necessary though they may be now, will not, I suggest, hasten the coming of the kind of world that we envisaged. There must, surely, be a stopping place somewhere in the arms race and military build up, a point where the futility of this mad struggle will dawn upon us and when, like the prodigal son, we will return to sanity.
Adequate defence is wise, but a constant struggle for greater and more potent weapons of destruction is nothing short of imbecility.
I think the suggestion of pooling our resources would involve the pooling of our scientific knowledge and skills. I think significant progress has been made in those things which contribute to human happiness, but it is a sad commentary on human intelligence that the greatest progress which has been made has been in the field of destructive capabilities. Who can estimate

External Affairs
the sum total of good which could accrue to the human race were all the skills and knowledge of men brought to bear upon constructive living, and if the results of scientific progress were made available to all people? Today, however, it appears that the great goal is to eclipse others in the technical field so that through these means our military capability will be increased. We now have the power to blast the nations into oblivion.
I ask the question: what more are we striving for? What is the object of scientific research and technological development? Is it to open the way for mankind into a fuller and more creatively worth-while life? If so, that is well and good. Is it to develop our capacity to destroy civilization with one bomb instead of two? If that is the case, it is devilish.
No doubt, this suggestion involves, also, to a certain degree at least, the pooling of economic resources. We have already referred to the Colombo plan and to the United Nations program for technical assistance, and I believe that it is the purpose of the nations which are gathered together in peaceful alliances not only to maintain themselves but to extend a helping hand to those who are in a less fortunate position than themselves. As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, we in this group have given full support to these programs and have urged that our contributions in this field should be extended. We still say that.
But let us ask a question here, as well. What is the motive behind the contributions which are being made to the under-developed countries? Is it to try and place them in a position of indebtedness to us, so that we, in turn, may expect their support in further programs that we may have? If our motives are unworthy they will soon become very obvious, and instead of buying support and buying friendliness they will bring instead antagonism and bitterness. If it is to feed the hungry, if it is to discharge our responsibility to those who are less fortunate than ourselves, and if we give gladly and willingly, without any hope or expectation-
How much did you give?

What was that asinine remark down there? Now, that is something. That is really something profound. We are dealing here with one of the greatest programs that we have for the betterment of mankind and then someone down in that end of the house raises that foolish question. Perhaps I should ask him what he gave.
Mr. Speaker, if it is to assist those who are in need, then I say: let us do our utmost,

increase our contributions and do everything we can to discharge our responsibility in this particular field.
I believe also that this co-operation and this pooling of our resources must include the pooling of our moral and spiritual resources also. There are certain features in soviet policy which we deeply deplore and one of them is the disparity between their preaching and their practice. But let us not imagine that they alone are guilty of this.
Down through the past we have been subjected to a tremendous peace offensive. In the past, as I have stated, we have been engaging in disarmament conferences and discussions. There has been the proclamation of the great principle of freedom for all men and the right of self-determination and sovereignty for all nations. Let us just think of this for a moment. I say we have been subjected to a great peace barrage and I suppose our views differ as to the sincerity of that peace offensive and what the purpose behind it all was. I believe it goes without saying that we are all in favour of peace but the only trouble is to find some way of making that dream a reality. That is the difficulty.
Much has been said and written about the self-determination of peoples and may I say that some of those who have been the loudest in proclaiming this doctrine have been the leaders of the Soviet union. However, while the so-called colonial powers of the west have been leading colonial peoples on toward the goal of nationhood and then standing by with moral and other support as those nations gained strength and confidence, the Soviet union stands out not only as the greatest colonial power but as the most ruthless of any who have ever held control over the minds and bodies of men, those peoples whom they profess to protect. As a matter of fact, some of the nations granted sovereignty by so-called western colonial powers are now struggling for their very existence against attempted communist domination.
Communism promises an era of peace and progress based upon the right of self-determination and mutual respect but institutes rather an iron rule that, while proclaiming the gospel of sovereignty and self-determination, proceeds to stifle the deepest aspirations of peoples and nations to live in freedom and dignity. Communism promises freedom from exploitation and a guarantee of civil rights but imposes a system which denies man the very freedoms which it professes to guarantee. We have many illustrations of this: the Ukraine, the Baltic states and the other satellite countries.

When men and nations reached the point of desperation and rose up ready and willing to sacrifice life and everything to try and regain their freedoms we had the illustration of the brutal suppression of the Hungarian people in their struggle for freedom and liberty.
Following the great conference of the communist nations we had the issue of this broad declaration: We are extending our hands to all people of good will. Jointly we will throw off the burden of armament which suppresses the people. We will free the world from the danger of war, death and destruction. Before us is a bright and happy future for mankind which is advancing toward progress. Hon. members will perhaps recognize these as the words of Mr. Khrushchev.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in order to demonstrate their sincerity there are two things which the Soviet union should do. The first is to settle down to a determined effort within the framework of the disarmament commission to work out a plan and program that would accomplish the very things they have been speaking about. I would also say that in order to prove their sincerity they should grant an opportunity to the nations under their control for a full and free expression of their wishes and desires relative to the system of government under which they choose to live. However, the leaders of the Soviet union are not the only ones who are guilty of hypocrisy for I believe that in assessing the world situation and striving for a solution we have to a large degree forgotten the application of the moral concept to our own activities.
There are two opposing forces in the world. On one hand we have a system of tyranny and oppression diametrically opposed to the way of life to which we pay lip service but unfortunately so often fail to practise, a totalitarian system in which the state is god and individuals are but pawns, a system characterized by suppression, fear and liquidation. On the other hand we have a system which extolls the glories of private enterprise and which recognizes the dignity of man and the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
In the past our whole attention has been devoted to an attempt to counter some move already made by communism in its bid for power and expansion, and in practically every case we have failed. What has happened is that in our hatred of communism we have begun to hate the communists. In our endeavour to contain communism we have become tragically negative in our approach to world problems. In our defence of the free way of life we have been almost ready
External Affairs
to sacrifice our freedoms. If we in our defence of freedom yield to a dictatorial regime nationally or internationally we shall become the victims of the very processes that we despise. We must not only require others to recognize and live according to the high principles of justice, honesty and humanity but we must scrupulously observe them ourselves, being sincere, fair and aboveboard in all our dealings with other nations. We must, I suggest, cleanse ourselves from uncharitable attitudes and ulterior motives and dedicate ourselves to the pursuit of those high principles in international affairs with courage, faith and determination. We must revitalize our democracy so that by a positive demonstration of the virtues of our system we will confound those who predict the deterioration and eventual collapse of the private enterprise economy. This will do much to strengthen the morale of our people and convince others how worth while is the democratic way of life.
I would now like to refer to what I understand has been the policy for many years in this house. Based on the idea that even though the full and free expression of party views could contribute greatly to the efficiency of internal parliamentary democracy, it was considered most desirable in so far as it was possible that our foreign policy should represent the united thought and attitude of parliament as a whole. Therefore, as nearly as possible, Canada followed a non-partisan policy in the field of foreign affairs.
I believe this desirable end may be secured or effected in different ways. Government could abdicate its responsibility and leave the formulation of policy to the non-partisan civil servants and career diplomats and both government and opposition view this as a good way out. That, of course, would be unthinkable. On the other hand, the opposition could abdicate its responsibility and for the sake of unanimity become "yes" men to government-sponsored policy. In closing my remarks I would like to propose another approach to this important question, namely the setting up of an all-party consultative committee with which the Secretary of State for External Affairs could confer with a view to acquainting himself with the views and proposals of the people's representatives.
In this way the elected representatives of the people could be kept informed of conditions and could have a part in recommending policy. We recognize, of course, that the minister and the government would of necessity have the final responsibility but, on the other hand, the opposition would retain their

External Affairs
right of criticism. Parliament also would exercise final control and the supremacy of parliament would be maintained in foreign affairs.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that such a committee should be composed of the leaders of the respective parties, with possibly the addition of one or more members from each of the groups. In this way I believe it would be possible for the setting forth of a truly Canadian policy with respect to foreign affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. Nesbitt (Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to extend to you my most sincere congratulations on your election to your very high office. It may come a little late but I have not had the opportunity of doing so before during this session.
It may appear, Mr. Speaker, from the latest dispatches, that the condition of President Eisenhower is perhaps not as grave as the information we received this afternoon led us to believe, and I would like to say on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and not only members on this side of the house but I am sure all members that we pray this is the case, that his condition is not so grave, and that this great leader of the free world will be restored to his accustomed vigour.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, in entering this debate on the subject of external affairs I propose to deal exclusively with the subject of disarmament which is a matter of the greatest interest and importance not only to the people of Canada but to people all over the world. I would like to take this opportunity of dealing with this subject because I have, in the last eight weeks, had the honour and the opportunity of serving as vicechairman of our delegation to the United Nations and of following the whole subject at first hand.
The disarmament negotiations of the subcommittee, which was held last summer in London, came to an abrupt end at the beginning of September after the soviet representative, Mr. Zorin, had rejected the proposals for partial measures of disarmament submitted by the four western powers in a working paper on August 29. This abrupt termination of the subcommittee's work was clearly a matter of great concern to many countries when the general assembly of the United Nations opened last September 17. The opening statements of all the great powers in the assembly reflected this concern. Speaking for Canada on September 23, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) expressed the hope that the current session of the United Nations assembly might be known in future years as a disarmament assembly.

These words were quoted with warmth by a number of successive speakers and I think the general tenor of the debate opened with fairly high hopes.
In general the debate concentrated upon the resolution of October 11, introduced by 24 of the major powers. Much of this resolution was based on the western proposals in the subcommittee on August 29. The subcommittee, of course, was held in London.
This afternoon the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) made a request of the Secretary of State for External Affairs asking that he deal with those proposals in detail and this evening I think I might outline the proposals of the 24-power resolution. They are condensed, of course, Mr. Speaker, but I think they reach the heart of the matter. This resolution was based upon six points which are as follows:
One. The immediate suspension of nuclear testing in conjunction with an adequate control system to ensure that this was carried out.
Two. The so-called "cut-off" or the cessation of the production of fissionable materials for weapons purposes.
Three. The reduction of stocks of nuclear weapons.
Four. The controlled and graduated reduction of armed forces and armaments; that is, conventional armaments, a field in which agreement had almost been reached.
Five. The progressive establishment of a ground and aerial system to guard against surprise attack.
Six. The study of an inspection system to ensure that objects would be sent into outer space only for peaceful and scientific purposes.
These six points presented a more complex resolution than any of those put forward by the U.S.S.K.; for they represented a series of concrete proposals on which the western powers and their allies in NATO had negotiated for months to ensure agreement. As a member of the subcommittee, Canada participated in the drafting of this resolution and co-sponsored it.
In contrast, the soviet resolutions were simple, propagandistic in their appeal and in their essence completely uncontrollable. Briefly, the Soviet union presented two proposals. The first was for a five-year ban on the use of nuclear weapons. This clearly meant nothing more than an uncontrollable promise which would be valid until the day it was broken. This resolution, I might say, received only 11 votes in favour.
The second soviet proposal called for the immediate cessation of testing, without regard

to any other measures on disarmament. It became quite evident that many nations were attracted by a proposal of this kind. India had submitted a very similar resolution and Japan presented a compromise resolution which linked the objective of a temporary suspension of nuclear testing to negotiations for an adequate supervision and inspection system to verify this. The Indian proposal received a vote of 22 for, 38 against and 20 abstentions. The Japanese proposal was opposed by the soviet bloc as well as by the west and was defeated by a vote of 18 for, 32 against and 31 abstentions. Canada voted against all these proposals because it felt, as did many other countries, that the question of nuclear test suspension can only be settled as a part of a more comprehensive disarmament agreement which also does something to solve the more fundamental matter of the arms race in nuclear weapons.
Perhaps because of the reservations which many countries had on matters such as nuclear test suspension, the disarmament debate showed little enthusiasm at the beginning. For some time there was a shortage of countries willing to speak; and while it was apparent that the 24-power resolution would receive an adequate majority many of the uncommitted nations questioned the value of requesting support by the assembly for what was essentially the position of one side to the cold war alone.
Many of our allies were slow to make public their support, as if they were waiting for some further clarification of the western position. For these reasons the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he delivered the Canadian statement in the committee on October 23 last, emphasized repeatedly that Canada, while it had sponsored the 24-power draft resolution and urged its adoption, remained open-minded. I should like to make a brief quotation from the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the political committee of the United Nations which was at that time discussing disarmament:
Canada is sensitive to every possibility of improving it. Let us not be inflexible in this regard. We of Canada certainly do not say that the particular proposals with which we are now associated are the only means by which at least some progress can be made toward disarmament. Canada has co-sponsored plans for partial disarmament, but I repeat that we do not necessarily regard them as the last word.
Canada's position of flexibility was enthusiastically welcomed by the representatives of many countries, including Norway, Mexico, Pakistan, Israel and Nepal. It was particularly noteworthy that in the closing remarks of the representative of the United States, Mr. Henry Cabot Lodge, he said that 96698-98
External Affairs
the United States associated itself at some length with the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Ambassador Lodge added that the United States also desired openmindedness and flexibility and they too were not suggesting that our proposals, the 24-power resolution, were the last word. It is perhaps not too much to say that this position of flexibility contributed to the large vote by which the 24-power resolution was passed. The resolution, incidentally, received 57 votes in favour, 9 votes against, being merely the soviet bloc, and 15 abstentions. This vote was later sustained when the resolution came from the political committee to the general assembly.
It would have been a very satisfactory result for the west and for Canada except for the dramatic soviet announcement just before the vote was taken that they would not return to participate in the work of either the disarmament commission or its subcommittee. Shortly before Russia had introduced a resolution calling for the establishment of a permanent disarmament commission consisting of all 82 members of the United Nations which would discuss disarmament continuously and without any secrecy whatsoever. It is hard to believe that the U.S.S.R. really wants such a commission or that this move was anything but a propaganda move. Only a few days earlier the soviets had argued that it would be wrong for the committee to vote for a disarmament agreement which should properly be the result of unanimous agreement among merely the great powers. Now the soviets appeared to be calling for a commission where just such votes would be taken all the time. One can only conclude that the soviets were resorting to their normal tactics of bargaining at an oriental bazaar; by demanding the impossible they were hoping to obtain a little more than they otherwise would.
The first reaction of Canada's allies was to discount the soviet intention to boycott the commission as an idle threat of no importance. This was not the Canadian reaction for we had always considered the composition of the disarmament commission and its subcommittee to be in question. One month earlier our Prime Minister, speaking of the disarmament subcommittee, had said in the assembly:
We consider that a salutary effect might be achieved by securing the participation of other powers; they may be capable of rendering assistance in the processes of seeking an agreement that we have not been able to achieve. But let me say this: Geography alone should not be the basis for choosing additional members, for all members are not equally equipped to contribute towards the agreement for which we all devotedly hope.

External Affairs
Some of our allies had said in the course of the debate that there should be no expansion either of the commission or its subcommittee, but we had been careful in our concluding remarks on November 4 last to keep our position open on this matter. Thus when the soviet made it clear that they would boycott the existing commission, we made strong representations to our allies that the question of commission expansion should be reconsidered. It was not-perhaps I should stress this point-a question of caving in to the Russians; it was not a question of doing something merely to bring them back to the disarmament negotiations. On these matters I think nearly everyone would agree that the Soviet union is inscrutable and, as events proved, they are quite capable of appearing to work for a compromise and then demanding something more, something quite unacceptable, when a compromise is offered them.
However, we felt that many countries in the United Nations were deeply concerned about the future of disarmament proceedings and that intransigence over a relatively small matter, the question of commission expansion, would appear in retrospect a foolish intransigence, particularly if it gave the U.S.S.R. a good excuse not to negotiate in the future at all. At this time many of our allies, unlike Canada, were under firm instructions to oppose expansion of the disarmament commission. Therefore, on November 6 we made only a guarded statement in the political committee just before the votes were taken. At that time I made certain remarks and I should like to quote what I said. I do so only because I think the remarks are pertinent to the remarks I am making at the moment. I said:
We do not believe that the size or composition of the disarmament commission and the subcommittee has been a major obstacle in the way of agreement. But, by the same token, we do not believe that a matter of some alteration in the United Nations disarmament bodies need inevitably be allowed to stand in the way of at least the opportunity for further negotiation. .	.	. Our
fundamental approach to a possible change in disarmament bodies was defined by Prime Minister Diefenbaker in his statement in the general debate on September 23. He made it clear at that time that we were certainly not opposed in principle to associating other countries with these disarmament talks if there was any chance that this would improve the prospects of success. If, however, the very possibility of continuing the negotiations at all is now jeopardized, then the willingness to accept some reasonable adjustment is all the more essential.
As we expected, this statement was warmly welcomed by many countries, including some of our NATO allies. Very shortly thereafter our allies on the subcommittee indicated to

us that they would not now be opposed to reasonable expansion of the disarmament commission.
The disarmament commission, I may say, is of course composed of the eleven members of the security council. In addition, Canada has the unique honour of being a permanent member of the commission, as well as of its subcommittee, whether or not she is a member of the security council. The western position in the security council has always been quite secure, as may be illustrated by the fact that nine of the eleven powers composing the newly elected security council voted for the western disarmament resolution at this assembly.
It was therefore agreed that some neutral or uncommitted countries, notably India, and some satellites such as Czechoslovakia, could be seated in the commission without any danger to the west. After this we were in constant consultation with the representatives of our three allies on the subcommittee. Ambassador Lodge for the United States, Commander Noble for the United Kingdom and Mr. Jules Moch for France.
At first it was agreed that an addition of five new members might be reasonable. Then immediately rumours of our negotiations began to spread, as they do down there, and many countries indicated that if there were to be any commission expansion then their own region, or more particularly their own country in some cases, should not be excluded. Thus, our subcommittee allies themselves asked that not five but ten countries should be added. These ten were Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Burma, Czechoslovakia, India, Italy, Tunisia and Yugoslavia.
It was agreed that if such a resolution for commission expansion were to be effective it should unite rather than divide the assembly, or at least that part of it outside the soviet bloc. Therefore, along with our allies we had been in constant consultation with India and with other leaders of the uncommitted nations. We had also had some contact, I may add, with the soviet delegation who had made it clear that they would not commit themselves to any resolution in advance. At times we seemed on the point of finding a list of countries which would be acceptable to all the powers concerned.
