However, after some days of negotiation it became more and more clear to the Canadian delegation that, regardless of our own views, it would be very hard to get prior agreement between all of our subcommittee allies on the one hand and the major uncommitted countries on the other. Therefore, in order to get the ship launched, so to speak, together with Japan we introduced a resolution calling upon the

assembly "to enlarge the disarmament commission by the addition of ten member states which, for the first year, from 1 January, 1958, to 1 January, 1959, shall be"-and then followed the ten countries I have previously mentioned. Our tactic on this occasion was, in the words of an eminent statesman of the past, to wait and see the reaction of the assembly to this resolution.
We were not surprised to learn that there was widespread feeling, even among some of our NATO allies, that while our resolution was a good thing it was perhaps not quite good enough, and that a more equitable and satisfactory list of countries could still be found. In short, Mr. Speaker, we continued to negotiate with the same intensity after our resolution was introduced as we had before. Twice the discussion of our resolution was postponed and once the assembly was adjourned for this purpose.
At length it became clear that India, Sweden and Yugoslavia would be satisfied with an amendment to our resolution which we ourselves had been considering, namely the addition of four more countries, Egypt, Mexico, Norway and Poland. When it was clear that this amendment could be accepted by all of our subcommittee allies we tabled a revised version of our resolution, one which was in our view very much more satisfactory and which would add all of these 14 countries and thus give the disarmament commission a membership of 25 countries. We were particularly pleased to obtain for our resolution the co-sponsorship of all the middle powers most concerned, namely Canada, India, Japan, Sweden and Yugoslavia. Later Paraguay joined the sponsors as a representative of Latin American countries.
At this point there was some reasonable optimism that in view of the wide sponsorship and support for our resolution, the U.S.S.R. would not oppose it and would indicate its return to the commission. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, this was the information that we and most of the other member nations of the assembly had received. However, such was not to be the case. At the last minute the soviet position hardened again and our resolution was honoured with a public rejection by the soviet representative to the United Nations. At the last minute the soviet tabled, in the name of Albania, an amendment calling for the addition of seven more countries. These countries were Austria, Bulgaria, Ceylon, Finland, Indonesia, Romania and Sudan, not one of which could truly be considered pro-western in its disarmament attitudes. The U.S.S.R. supported 96698-98J
External Affairs
this resolution in all seriousness as an effective "compromise" to meet the western position "half-way". They made a firm statement that only if this unacceptable amendment were accepted would they return to the disarmament commission, a statement which led most countries to conclude that the U.S.S.R. simply did not wish to turn to the commission at all.
The voting on our resolution and on the soviet proposal showed that the Soviet union had allowed itself to become completely isolated on this matter. Many "neutral" countries were offended by this abrupt soviet rejection of a serious negotiated compromise on which much labour had been expended. Yugoslavia in particular expressed its regret that our resolution had not been generally accepted. Because of this disappointment Yugoslavia declined to vote on the resolution in any way. After the Albanian amendment had been defeated by a vote of 19 for and 38 against, with 19 abstentions, our resolution was then passed by the impressive majority of 60 for to 9 against, with 11 abstentions. Only the hard core of the soviet bloc voted against our resolution. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that our resolution was supported by most of the Asian countries and almost the entire Arab group, including Egypt, Jordan and Syria. The soviet proposal for a permanent 82 member commission received only the 9 votes of its own bloc.
If the U.S.S.R. persists in its refusal to negotiate, one may well ask what Canada's efforts in this matter have achieved. I think that question was probably in the mind of the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) when he made his remarks this afternoon. We have at the very least shown a constructive willingness to make reasonable concessions in order to continue serious talks on this vitally urgent question. No one can say that western stubborness on the mere machinery of United Nations disarmament talks has been an obstacle to progress. For a long time there has been in the assembly a feeling that, due to the composition of the security council on which it is based, the disarmament machinery has been heavily weighted towards the western point of view. This was a genuine issue, one which prompted the remarks of the Prime Minister in the assembly. In the light of the soviet position, many countries felt it imperative to remedy this matter, if only to reassure countries all over the world of the sincerity of the western desire for a negotiated disarmament agreement. That has been done, and many countries are now looking forward to playing a constructive, if small, role in the complex negotiations which must still take place.

External Affairs
It would, of course, serve no constructive end to allow the commission to become a mere sounding board for soviet propaganda. In our negotiations we were constantly mindful of this danger. But since the passage of our resolution all of our subcommittee allies have indicated to us that they have no misgivings at all about the composition of the new commission. On the contrary, they are glad to welcome countries which ought, in their opinion, to be able to learn more of the complex issues involved in this great question of disarmament.
The point has been made by the hon. member for Algoma East that if agreement could not be reached in a committee of five, it cannot be expected in a committee of 25. This compares the old subcommittee of the disarmament commission with the new disarmament commission as a whole. Perhaps I did not understand the hon. member's remarks this afternoon, but that was the interpretation I took from them.
The new larger disarmament commission of 25 members does not rule out further meetings of a smaller subcommittee. If the major powers concerned will agree, there can be further meetings of the old, indeed of a new, subcommittee. There was also in New York a Mexican proposal for a subcommittee to meet under a special chairman such as the president of the general assembly. This too would be by no means unacceptable to us if the major powers would agree to it. However, during the recent weeks of meetings of the general assembly it did not appear that this proposal was acceptable to any of the major powers, nor indeed did it appear to be acceptable to anyone else in the assembly. The problem was to find machinery acceptable to all or, failing that, to offer a reasonable compromise to make our desire for further negotiations on disarmament abundantly clear.
One can still ask whether the Soviet union can afford to boycott a commission where countries like India, Egypt and Yugoslavia have come to hear the U.S.S.R. defend its position on disarmament. Thanks to our resolution, if the U.S.S.R. does boycott the commission it will no longer have any respectable reason for doing so. It will certainly not endear itself to these uncommitted countries; while the west, on the other hand, will be in a position to make its point of view much more clearly understood.
In the voting on our resolution, the U.S.S.R. was already isolated from these uncommitted countries. Many other countries have approached us to express their gratitude and relief that a sound and constructive resolution to expand the commission was introduced and passed. For this means that the

assembly has done what it could to further disarmament negotiations; and the onus is now squarely on the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics to justify its position. Even the U.S.S.R. cannot continually fly in the face of world public opinion, and particularly public opinion in those uncommitted parts of the world in Asia and Africa. Since the end of world war II the U.S.S.R. has been attempting to gain the sympathetic public and official support of these new Asian and African countries in order to further her plans for ultimate world control. If the U.S.S.R. continues to act as she did on the disarmament question as well as in the recent Syrian situation referred to this afternoon in the remarks made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and in the Hungarian affair of scarcely a year ago, she-that is the Soviet union-will not long continue to enjoy much public or official support in the neutralist countries in Asia or Africa.
By having exposed the true motives and behaviour of the U.S.S.R. to the peoples of the uncommitted countries of Asia and Africa and indeed everywhere, we have done much not only to prevent further Russian advances in the world struggle for men's minds but we have indeed, in my opinion, forced her to give ground.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house listened with interest this afternoon to the first statement on foreign affairs by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith). While we cannot all share in domestic matters the same political views, he has given us a good example today, as he did on the day when he was sworn in, of the possibility of a maximum measure of unity between all political parties in the important matter of our relations to other nations in the world.
No doubt it was part of this desire to transend political divisions which caused him to remind us again of the signal recognition given to one of our number in this house, the former secretary of state for external affairs who recently was awarded the Nobel peace prize. I would like, as a colleague of the member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), to take the opportunity in this particular debate to say that those of us on this side of the house join with the Secretary of State for External Affairs in noting our pride and satisfaction at the recognition of the efforts of his predecessor, over a long period, in the cause of peace.
I think it is appropriate that I should utter these words because, except for the right hon. gentleman who leads the official opposition, possibly I have had a better opportunity than anyone else in this house to know how

deserving has been the hon. member for .Algoma East to become the recipient of a Nobel award. I have served with him on many occasions at the United Nations, both when he was president of the assembly and when he was chairman of the political committee of the United Nations, as well as in other fields of endeavour in international affairs, and I can attest in all sincerity to the fact that he, above all others, is deserving of this recognition given to him in succession to such great figures in foreign affairs as Aristide Briand, the former minister of foreign affairs for France; Frank Kellogg, the former secretary of state for foreign affairs in the United States-(co-authors of the Kellogg-Briand pact)-Dr. Albert Schweitzer and of course Dr. Ralph Bunche. I think it is also appropriate that I should say, as one who on behalf of some hon. members recently had conversations with the secretary general of the United Nations with regard to his coming to Canada to join with us in marking this recognition, that the secretary general regrets events of the moment necessitate his departure for Europe. And so he will be unable to share with members of this house the privilege of paying tribute to the honourable member for Algoma East.
The country, and I know the house, welcomes the appointment of the hon. gentleman to a portfolio which, until his appointment, was held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), a busy Prime Minister whose preoccupations, understandably, in so many fields of action did not in the judgment of many people commend the retention by him of the administration of external affairs. This is particularly so at a time when the international situation is so tenuous, so tense, and so difficult of solution.
We have, I think, because of the complexity of modern day events, realized that the decision of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King to have a separate minister in charge of external affairs was indeed a wise one. It is not possible under the circumstances obtaining in the world and which now confront us for anyone to hold the portfolio of Secretary of State for External Affairs as a sideline. We all therefore welcomed the decision of the Prime Minister to appoint a fulltime minister of this important department. I am sure the hon. gentleman will bring to his task the qualities of intellect and heart which he possesses, and that he will pursue these matters of vital moment, with skill and tact.
As he narrated this afternoon, one could not help but conclude that basically he is carrying out a policy already laid down by his predecessor. He recognizes, of course, the
External Affairs
value of the United Nations but he, too, recognizes that Canadian foreign policy is predicated upon the fact that we are a member of the commonwealth of nations, that we are a neighbour of a great world power, the United States, and that we are an active member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. These four affiliations, it seems to me, have characterized the basic foundations of foreign policy in this country. I believe all of us recognize that while there is a difference between our affiliation or our relationship to the commonwealth and the United States of America-important as are both those relationships-we do not in any way deprecate the importance of the United Nations. This principle was set forth-as we were reminded by the member for Algoma East, this afternoon-by the Prime Minister himself in the statement made by him on September 23 of this year. He said that the support of the United Nations is the cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy. The Prime Minister continued:
We believe that the United Nations will grow stronger because it represents the inevitable struggle of countries to find order in their relationships and the deep longing of mankind to strive for and attain peace and justice.
Those words, somewhat similar to those uttered by the former prime minister, I believe represent the conviction of most members of this house and that of the great majority of the Canadian people, in the present and ultimate purposes of the organization which arise from the charter signed at San Francisco in 1945. The United Nations may not be the perfect instrument to preserve order among the nations, but it does represent in the international sphere the same kind of instrument which in the course of history, the community has developed to preserve order in the domestic realm. It is one to which we must give our continued support along the lines laid down by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Canada can play, notwithstanding the fact that she is not one of the great powers, an increasingly important role as was demonstrated during the past decade by the former secretary of state for external affairs and the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent).
My own connection with the United Nations goes back to the first meeting at Church House in 1946 when I went to the United Nations under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition, and again with that right hon. gentleman to the second part of the general assembly of the United Nations, also in 1946. As I have paid inadequate but deserving tribute to one of my

External Affairs
colleagues, I think the house would want me to say that we also recognize that the former prime minister and the present Leader of the Opposition, one of those who proposed the concept of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, will be remembered in this house and in this country, not only for his contribution to the development of Canada, but for his great contribution to the maintenance of peace in the world.
We will take the opportunity now, because of our membership on the security council, to play an increasingly important role, because the political questions which come before that body-a body which has, in this particular, a primacy of interest and authority-will afford to Canada and to its representative an opportunity of conciliation and mediation not open to us, except during the course of the general assembly, since the time we were last a member of the security council, when our representative was General McNaughton.
Hon. members will recall the important contribution which General McNaughton made on a number of matters, not the least being the constructive role he played in carving out national status for Indonesia. Likewise, our representative on the security council will have the opportunity of playing a useful role in matters of consequence, in a sense the kind of role signalized this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he referred to the work of the international commissions in Indochina, Laos and Vietnam.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs did not mention the situation in Cambodia where an international commission also operates. If I understood the Secretary of State for External Affairs correctly, the work of this international commission has been completed. I do not know whether or not the commission is to be disbanded but, if I may, I would suggest to the hon. minister, based on the experience of my visit to Indochina last year, that there is a role which the commission can play apart from its precise terms of reference; there are opportunities, possibly, for some form of continued action in the light, particularly, of the kind of situation which prevails in South and North Vietnam.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. member for Essex East would permit me to correct an impression, which, evidently, I made upon him this afternoon? I did not intend to say, and I do not think I said, that the international commission would be abandoned. I did intimate to the house that the task of the commission in Cambodia is about completed. The other

international commissions in Laos and Vietnam still have work to do.

I thank the
Secretary of State for External Affairs for that correction. Likely the error was mine, not his. But I had the impression a year ago that the situation in South Vietnam was such that that kind of international body could serve a desired purpose. But my reference to it is largely to point out that a country like Canada can play a useful role, not only at the United Nations but in keeping the peace, as these commissions have obviously done in all three countries of the old Indochina.
I do not know whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs was too enthusiastic in the conclusions he reached about Laos, but in any event I am sure he is aware of the implications that flow from the integration of the Pathet Lao with the royal government. This is a matter which requires great scrutiny, having in mind the need to preserve the integrity, not only of Laos but of South Vietnam, and of Cambodia and countries like Thailand in the neighbouring area.
We listened a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, to a detailed and interesting account of recent disarmament discussions in the general assembly given by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). I think the house would wish me to say to him how grateful we are for this report of his endeavours. The question of disarmament does not necessarily mean that the continuation of heavy armaments is in itself a necessary provocation for conflict. The high level of armaments is rather a reflection of the condition of our world than a cause of those conditions. In any event, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) said this afternoon, it must be the aim of governments by all means within their power always observing the requirements of security, to do everything they can to ease the heavy burden placed on their peoples by high defence expenditures.
But I think we must bear in mind that this situation is not one of our making. The kind of world in which we live demands, at this stage, certainly, strength of arms in the face of the might of that group of communist nations which confronts us in almost every sphere of international action. In the face of this situation there can certainly be no unilateral disarmament. That mistake we made once before. But just as we have learned that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has served as an insurance premium against aggression, I think we must recognize that difficult as it is, we must be practical in our

assessment of the need for armaments and for defence arrangements at this time.
However, I repeat we must seize every opportunity at the United Nations and elsewhere to resolve some of the great political problems which confront us, all of which have their bearing on whether or not it would be possible to bring about any specific measure of disarmament. The present disarmament discussions arose, I suspect, out of the decision of the Soviet union in September, 1954, when that country announced it had abandoned the position which it had taken since the end of the second world war. No longer, Andrei Vishinski said, would the Soviet union insist on an agreement to ban the use and production of atomic weapons as a condition precedent to disarmament in the conventional arms field. And it was that important declaration of the abandonment of a principle, which had stood in the way of any progress whatsoever during the preceding 10 years, which gave some encouragement to the possibility of arriving at some agreement through the subcommittee of five of the disarmament commission in the fall of 1954. That subcommittee is an agent of the disarmament commission itself, which had its genesis in the first meetings of the United Nations. This subcommittee was created- and this should be remembered in the light of what has just been said-primarily to provide a more efficient way of providing a forum for discussion of disarmament objectives. It was said, and argued, that the only way to provide discussion of disarmament was to see that it took place among those nations on whose shoulders rested the primary responsibility, namely the great powers. These meetings were to be held in camera. In this way it was hoped there might ensue a comprehensive agreement on disarmament.
I served on the disarmament committee over a period of two years. I think I can speak with some experience of the nature of those discussions and of the problems involved. I do not propose to go into any detail, but may I say that once it was evident that the Soviet union had abandoned its original position of insisting on the prohibition of the manufacture and use of atomic weapons as a condition precedent to action in the conventional field, an effort was made to try to get some limitation in the number of armed forces which would be available to the five countries represented on the subcommittee, namely, the United States, the United Kingdom, France, the Soviet union and Canada.
It looked at one time as though it was going to be possible to arrive at some limitation of armaments and that we were going to be able to get an agreement; for instance, that
External Affairs
the Soviet union would be limited to 2,500,000 men and the United States to a similar limitation, Great Britain and France to 650,000 and countries like Canada to something like 250,000. But one of the essential conditions laid down was that at every step there should be in existence some organ of control that would include inspection, not initially air inspection but certainly ground inspection. In any event the position taken by the western nations was that we must first of all agree on what were the objects of control and then we must decide on the methods by which the control system was to be operated. The concept of control, we thought, need not be complete; it need be no greater than the stage by stage process agreed on. In any event there must be some control body and the methods necessary to make that control effective must be agreed upon in advance. There should be no reliance merely on the good faith of the Soviet union, we argued.
I agree with what the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said. The reason we have not had any real success in this matter lies largely at the doorstep of the Soviet union which at no time was willing to give any indication of its concept of what the objects of control were or what steps should be taken to make that control effective. That will be found not as a matter of obiter dictum by those of us who participated in these discussions; it is a matter of record that at every turn when these requests for these indications were put the Soviet union was unwilling to give an answer which would give some justification for feeling that at least in one stage or in one step some progress could be made without violating the conditions of national security.
We were confronted not only with the control of conventional arms but the more difficult question of the control of nuclear weapons. The house will recall that in July of 1955 the heads of the governments of the four great powers met in Geneva. Because of the difficulties of control and because it was recognized by the Soviet union and by the United States through Premier Bulganin and President Eisenhower that it was not possible to control nuclear weapons that question had to be shelved. In the meantime it was agreed that some effort should be made at reaching a partial agreement on disarmament. Let me repeat, it was because the complete * elimination of nuclear weapons could not at that time be effectively controlled or made part of any program of disarmament capable of implementation in the foreseeable future that President Eisenhower, as a means of

External Affairs
creating a healthier international climate, suggested a method to avoid the dangers of a surprise attack.
The house will recall that that proposal involved the exchange of military blueprints as well as affording to both sides the opportunity of aerial inspection. The proposal was not accepted by the Soviet union although it was accepted at that time in principle by Canada and accepted by the prime minister of this country in greater detail during the course of the last summer.
The history of this matter then is that if we have not succeeded in reducing armaments we must blame the intransigent position taken by the Soviet union. This does not mean that the fault is all on one side nor am I suggesting that. I say now as a private member that I think it is regrettable more consideration was not given two years ago, not only to dealing with the question of armaments in being but with the question of weapons not then in existence. We are now in the age of the intercontinental ballistic missile. Its significance for the world of course needs no comment by me. The position of countries like the United Kingdom only 800 miles away, and countries now within the reach of missiles with a travel power of 5,000 miles speaks eloquently for the potential power of this new instrument of war.
The proposal was then made-and this was along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-that the scientists of the world dealing with outer space and with future satellites and the like should foregather under international auspices, just as they did in Geneva in 1955 prior to the setting up of the atomic energy agency, to see if they could not pool their knowledge in the hope of avoiding the terrible installations of war that are now apparently a fact. Well, that is all history but it does in part reflect the reluctance and I believe the unwillingness of the Soviet union to recognize that this development, costly and burdensome as it is on the peoples of the world and diverting as it does our resources from more constructive purposes, gave the Soviet union the opportunity of making the contribution which their leaders now say they are prepared to do and which they urge can now be done in new meetings and in new peace pacts. I believe that the world does not want new peace pacts; what it wants is a determination on the part of the Soviet union to live up to the commitments to which she has already obligated herself. That is the way, it seems to me, to begin to deal with the situations that confront us.
The hon. member for Algoma East this afternoon raised another question to which

I would like to devote a few moments. He referred to the matter of continental air defence known as NORAD, the defence of the North American continent, now under the command of General Partridge of the United States air force. No one will quarrel with the importance of this particular objective. While all the details are not known to us, and on that account do not endow us with the opportunity of passing a final judgment as to merit, it would seem at least that the objective the government had in mind in the concurrence it has given is one to which there can in principle certainly be no exception taken. Indeed in this thermonuclear age the only way we can defend ourselves, as we learned in 1947 when we set up NATO, is by some common defensive arrangement among likeminded nations. Certainly the defence of this continent presupposes common action between the United States and Canada. Therefore, any observations that we make on this side with regard to this matter or any questions we put have nothing whatsoever to do with the objective of preserving and guaranteeing the maximum measure of defence for the North American continent.
We are a nation dedicated to the principle of parliamentary democracy and under our system of government while the cabinet, the executive, is responsible for the formulation of foreign policy and also responsible for its execution, nevertheless either during the stage of negotiation-and that is a matter to be determined by the government-or after negotiations have been concluded and policies decided on it is the obligation of government under our parliamentary tradition to submit its policies to the representatives of the people for approval.
We are not asking the government to let this parliament decide on policy. We recognize that it is the responsibility of government alone to decide policy, but once they have decided, parliament has the right to be informed, to be given the opportunity of approving or disapproving. That opportunity has not been given to us in this matter. In fairness to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), this particular arrangement is of an interim character, as he himself says. What is that interim arrangement? We have not been told about it. We are entitled to know how it was reached. As the former secretary of state for external affairs said today, while we have no right to ask what discussion has taken place in cabinet, we have the right to know whether or not there was a discussion in cabinet on this matter. We have the right to-
May I ask a question? The hon. member will recall that the Prime Minister said this matter had been discussed in cabinet.

What the Prime Minister said in answer to the questions I put to him was that this represented the policy of the government as a whole. That was the reply of the Prime Minister to my question. Was this matter discussed in cabinet? Was this matter discussed in the defence committee? When I asked these questions exception was taken to them. The Prime Minister told us later that the pattern being followed in this matter was the same as that we had followed in the matter of the Ogdensburg agreement which followed the discussions between the president of the United States and Mr. Mackenzie King in 1940. Again the North Atlantic Treaty Organization had been decided on by the government of the day as a matter of policy, and later that treaty was submitted to parliament for approval. Contrary to what the Prime Minister did say, the Ogdensburg agreement likewise was submitted to parliament; it was submitted to parliament on November 12, 1940, by the right hon. prime minister of that day. He outlined not only the terms of the agreement but the conversations that began a few months previously at Hyde Park with the president of the United States, and he also indicated something which has not been yet indicated by the Minister of National Defence.

May I ask
the hon. member a question? He just made the remark that the prime minister of the day introduced the debate in the House of Commons in August, 1940, and then he went on to say that the conversations had taken place a few months previously at Hyde Park. How much had parliament learned in the meantime?

If my hon. friend will look at the debate he will see that parliament was told everything. There is a difference between conversations in the stage of negotiation which had yielded no decisions and conversations which resulted in actual agreements.
I argued a few moments ago that no one expects the government, in the conduct of its foreign policy, during negotiations to reveal the details of those negotiations. No one contends that; but what I am saying is this. What the prime minister of that day did, as a result of his discussions at Ogdensburg with the president of the United States, was to give the information to parliament at the earliest possible opportunity. He outlined for parliament the nature of those discussions and the agreement concluded.
External Affairs
Agreement made in August.

All right, let me finish this. I asked the Minister of National Defence whether before the present government arrived at its decision, did it, let us say, as a matter of courtesy-although I think it could be put on much stronger grounds- advise Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom? My hon. friend has not yet replied to that question. In the case of the Ogdensburg agreement, the prime minister of the day pointed out at page 56 of Hansard that His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom had been apprised of the nature of the discussions with the president of the United States.
I am not suggesting that there is any constitutional necessity for doing so, but in the matter of collaboration, particularly in matters of defence, it seems to be the elementary thing to do, namely to discuss such matters with one's associates, one's allies. We asked the government, was there an order in council giving effect to the decision arrived at? Was there a minute of council?
And, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that when we asked for a minute, on reflection I thought that I should not persist in that request, that possibly it was an improper one. But on further reflection, I do not think it was because I find that on November 12, 1940, the prime minister of that day, in reporting on the Ogdensburg agreement, actually tabled in parliament the minute of cabinet by which this matter was decided on by the executive arm of government.
In this particular matter, a matter of the greatest importance to this nation, we have no document whatsoever, no interim agreement, no order in council, no minute of cabinet.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes that are left tonight I have one or two things that I should like to say. In the first place, I should like to add my congratulations to those of others to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) on the assumption of his post and taking his seat in the house, and also to congratulate the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) on his receipt of the Nobel peace prize. But I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was very disappointed that neither the present Secretary of State for External Affairs nor the former secretary of state for external affairs gave to the parliament of Canada this afternoon any comprehensive survey of the world situation in which we find ourselves today. We had instead a rather limited account of certain actions in the United Nations. We had some very smart political footwork from the former secretary of state for external affairs, but it does seem to me that the people of Canada are asking for something better than that today.
I believe that the people of Canada are asking for the type of thing to which the leader of the C.C.F. referred this afternoon when he referred to Mr. George Keenan's statement with regard to the solution of problems in Europe. I believe the people of Canada will find a note in Dr. Hugh Keenley-side's recent speech that will strike a responsive chord, and I think that now is the time when both the government of the day and the official opposition should be taking a very serious look at the world in which we find ourselves to decide whether or not Canada's role should be entirely different from that which we have pursued in the past.
I believe we have to ask ourselves certain questions and to abide by the logic of the answers. The first question that I suggest we have to ask ourselves is, do we consider that the Soviet union is preparing at any time to launch a military war of aggression on the rest of the world or do we consider that the evidence points in the other direction? Many spokesmen in eminent places in the world have of recent months reached the conclusion that there is no evidence to support the idea that the rulers of the Soviet union are so insane that they are preparing to launch a war that must be as destructive to themselves as to the west.

If we agree with that point of view, Mr. Speaker, then I think we have to ask ourselves another question. In the light of that assessment of the situation, what is the most useful role that Canada can play in order to relieve the present extremely dangerous world tensions? I was thinking earlier this evening when we heard a long report on the abortive disarmament discussions at the United Nations that perhaps we are barking up the wrong tree entirely when we imagine that it is possible by such discussions to bring about a disarmament program without having previously allayed those tensions in the world which have caused the armament race. I think perhaps we are trying to put the cart before the horse, and I believe history bears me out on that.
I have lived long enough to remember repeated occasions upon which there were attempts to stop earlier armament races and on no occasions were those attempts successful. They were not successful in those earlier periods. There was always the possibility of military success in carrying out national policy and if there is a possibility today of reaching some agreement on disarmament it can only be on the basis that there is no longer that possibility of military victory.
I suggest, sir, that we should take another and rather realistic look, not without regard to our national pride, as to just how important a role Canada can play in actual fact in the military situation in the world today. I think we have to admit that our role will be almost imperceptible no matter what efforts we might put into it. What we are facing is two giants poised in an extremely dangerous position and because all our sympathies, shall I say, lie with one of those giants, is no reason in my opinion for us imagining that we are serving the cause of peace by tying ourselves to the policies of that one great power. In fact, it seems to me that we have a duty towards our friends in the United States to aid them in extricating themselves from the extremely dangerous position in which they find themselves today.
I suggest, sir, along the lines suggested by the leader of this group earlier this evening, that Canada should turn her attention to other serious matters in the world rather than making and continuing what are now admittedly ineffectual attempts to make a worth-while and significant contribution to the war between the giants. All the areas of the world that are undeveloped at the present time are in fact the most important sections of th,e world today because it is on the decisions made in those nations that will depend whether or not the spirit of democracy or totalitarianism is going to prevail in 96698-99J

Mr. G. K. Fraser (Peterborough) presented the first and second reports of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and moved that the first report be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
